enc.title: Sheet 1 Q1: Compton effect

source.where: Exercise sheet I, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 1.pdf

enc.goal: (i) Thomson: an electron at rest in the field $\vec E=\vec\varepsilon E_0\cos(kx-\omega t)$ obeys $m\ddot{\vec x}=-e\vec E$ (magnetic force neglected). Solve it; what is the frequency of the emitted light? (ii) Compton: treat light as photons, $(cp_1,\vec p_1)$, $\lambda_1=h/p_1$, scattering elastically off the electron by an angle $\theta$. Show $\lambda_2=\lambda_1+\frac{h}{mc}(1-\cos\theta)$. (iii) In which limit is Thomson scattering recovered, and for which light is the Compton effect observable?

steps.reveal: With $\vec k\parallel\hat e_3$ the motion is transverse: $\vec x(t)=-\frac{eE_0}{m\omega^2}\vec\varepsilon(1-\cos\omega t)$. The electron oscillates at $\omega$ and radiates as a dipole at the same frequency $\omega$: no frequency shift classically.
steps.explain:
Why the field is just $\cos\omega t$. The electron moves very little compared with the wavelength, so in $\cos(kx-\omega t)$ we can set $x\approx0$: the electron feels a uniform field oscillating in time. Then $\ddot{\vec x}=-\frac{eE_0}{m}\vec\varepsilon\cos\omega t$; integrate twice with $\vec x(0)=\dot{\vec x}(0)=0$.

The physics: a charge shaken at $\omega$ radiates at $\omega$. Classical light is re-emitted at the same colour, whatever the angle.

steps.reveal: $(cp_1,\vec p_1)+(mc^2,0)=(cp_2,\vec p_2)+(\sqrt{m^2c^4+p^2c^2},\vec p)$. Eliminate the electron: $p^2=p_1^2-2p_1p_2\cos\theta+p_2^2$ (momentum), and from the energy $(p_1-p_2+mc)^2=m^2c^2+p^2$. Together $2p_1p_2(1-\cos\theta)=2mc(p_1-p_2)$; divide by $p_1p_2$ and use $\lambda=h/p$.
steps.explain:
Strategy: two conservation laws (energy, momentum), and we do not care about the electron afterwards, so eliminate it. Momentum: $\vec p=\vec p_1-\vec p_2$, square it (law of cosines): $p^2=p_1^2+p_2^2-2p_1p_2\cos\theta$. Energy: $cp_1+mc^2=cp_2+\sqrt{m^2c^4+p^2c^2}$; isolate the root and square: $(p_1-p_2+mc)^2=m^2c^2+p^2$.

Combine: expanding the left side, $p_1^2$, $p_2^2$ and $m^2c^2$ cancel against the right side, leaving $2mc(p_1-p_2)=2p_1p_2(1-\cos\theta)$. Divide by $p_1p_2\,mc$: $\frac1{p_2}-\frac1{p_1}=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{mc}$, and $\lambda=h/p$ turns this into the shift.

steps.reveal: The shift is at most $2h/mc$ with $\lambda_C=h/mc=2.42\times10^{-12}$ m. For $\lambda\gg\lambda_C$ (visible light, $10^{-7}$ m) the relative change is negligible: Thomson. Only hard X-rays and $\gamma$-rays show it.
steps.explain: Compare scales. The shift is at most $2\lambda_C\approx5\times10^{-12}$ m whatever the light. Relative to visible light ($\sim5\times10^{-7}$ m) that is $10^{-5}$: invisible, and the photon picture reduces to the classical one. Only when $\lambda$ is itself of order picometres (X-rays, gamma rays) is the change noticeable.

enc.title: Sheet 1 Q2: Bohr atom

source.where: Exercise sheet I, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 1.pdf

enc.goal: Bohr: $mv_nr_n=n\hbar$, $r_n=\frac{n^2\hbar^2}{me^2}$ (Gaussian units). (i) With $\lambda=h/p$ show $\lambda/r_n=2\pi/n$: the wave fits around the orbit. (ii) Show $v_n\ll c$. (iii) Show that the emitted wavelength (e.g. $n=\infty\to1$) is much larger than the Bohr radius.

steps.reveal: $\frac{\lambda}{r_n}=\frac{h}{mv_nr_n}=\frac{2\pi\hbar}{n\hbar}=\frac{2\pi}n$: $n$ wavelengths fit on the circumference.
steps.explain: Insert de Broglie $\lambda=h/(mv_n)$ and divide by $r_n$: the denominator is $mv_nr_n$, which Bohr's rule sets to $n\hbar$. With $h=2\pi\hbar$: $\lambda=2\pi r_n/n$, i.e. the circumference holds exactly $n$ wavelengths. Bohr's mysterious rule is a standing-wave condition.

steps.reveal: $v_n=\frac{n\hbar}{mr_n}=\frac{e^2}{n\hbar}\le v_1=\alpha c=2.19\times10^6$ m/s $\ll c$ ($\alpha\approx1/137$).
steps.explain: From $mv_nr_n=n\hbar$: $v_n=n\hbar/(mr_n)$; insert $r_n$: $v_n=e^2/(n\hbar)$. The largest is $n=1$, and $e^2/\hbar=\alpha c$ with $\alpha\approx1/137$: under 1% of the speed of light, so non-relativistic QM is fine for hydrogen.

steps.reveal: $E_n=-13.6\ \mathrm{eV}/n^2$, $\lambda_{nm}=\frac{hc}{E_n-E_m}\ge\lambda_{\infty1}=\frac{hc}{13.6\ \mathrm{eV}}\approx91$ nm $\gg a_0=0.053$ nm: the atom is tiny compared with its light (dipole approximation).
steps.explain: The shortest emitted wavelength belongs to the largest energy jump, $n=\infty\to1$, i.e. $13.6$ eV: $\lambda=hc/13.6\,\mathrm{eV}\approx91$ nm. That is a thousand times the atom's size. So the light's field is practically uniform across the atom; this is why the dipole approximation works.

questions.title: Galilei invariance of the Schrödinger equation

enc.title: Sheet 1 Q3: Galilei invariance of the Schrödinger equation

source.where: Exercise sheet I, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 1.pdf

enc.goal: If $\Psi(x,t)$ solves the free Schrödinger equation $i\hbar\partial_t\Psi=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2\Psi$, show that $\Psi_u(x,t)=\Psi(x-ut,t)\exp\left[\frac{im}{\hbar}ux-\frac{im}{2\hbar}u^2t\right]$ is a solution for every constant $u$.

steps.reveal: $i\hbar\partial_t\Psi_u=\left[i\hbar\partial_t\Psi-i\hbar u\,\partial_x\Psi+\frac m2u^2\Psi\right]e^{imu(x-ut/2)/\hbar}$ (arguments $x-ut,t$), and $i\hbar\partial_t\Psi=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2\Psi$.
steps.explain:
What is being checked: moving with velocity $u$ (a Galilean boost) must map solutions to solutions. Physically a boosted particle is shifted by $ut$ and has extra momentum $mu$; the phase $e^{imux/\hbar}$ supplies that momentum.

The time derivative hits three places: $\Psi$ through its first argument $x-ut$ (gives $-u\partial_x\Psi$), through its second argument $t$, and the phase (gives $-\frac{imu^2}{2\hbar}$). Multiply by $i\hbar$.

steps.reveal: $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2\Psi_u=\left[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2\Psi-i\hbar u\,\partial_x\Psi+\frac m2u^2\Psi\right]e^{imu(x-ut/2)/\hbar}$: identical. The phase $e^{imux/\hbar}$ is the boost of the momentum by $mu$.
steps.explain: Two $x$-derivatives of a product (product rule twice): $\partial_x^2\Psi$, a cross term $2\cdot\frac{imu}{\hbar}\partial_x\Psi$ and $\left(\frac{imu}{\hbar}\right)^2\Psi$. Multiplying by $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}$ gives exactly the same three terms as the time side; the $\partial_x^2\Psi$ and $i\hbar\partial_t\Psi$ terms match because $\Psi$ itself solves the equation.

keyPoints: both sides give the same three terms

enc.title: Sheet 2 Q1: Ehrenfest’s theorem

source.where: Exercise sheet II, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 2.pdf

enc.goal: Prove $m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\langle x\rangle=-\langle V^\prime(x)\rangle$ for motion in a potential $V$. Hint: bring $\frac{d}{dt}\langle x\rangle$ into a form proportional to $\Psi\overleftrightarrow{\partial_x}\Psi^*$.

steps.reveal: With the Schrödinger equation, $\frac{d}{dt}\langle x\rangle=\frac{i\hbar}{2m}\int x\,\partial_x(\Psi^*\partial_x\Psi-\Psi\partial_x\Psi^*)dx=-\frac{i\hbar}{2m}\int(\Psi^*\partial_x\Psi-\Psi\partial_x\Psi^*)dx=\frac{\langle p\rangle}{m}$ (integration by parts, no boundary terms).
steps.explain: Where it comes from. $\frac{d}{dt}\langle x\rangle=\int x\,\partial_t|\Psi|^2dx$, and the Schrödinger equation turns $\partial_t|\Psi|^2$ into $-\partial_xj$ (probability flows). One integration by parts moves the derivative off the current onto $x$ ($\partial_xx=1$); the boundary terms vanish for a normalisable $\Psi$. What remains, $\int j\,dx$, is $\langle p\rangle/m$.

steps.reveal: $\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\langle x\rangle=\frac1m\int\left[(H\Psi)^*\partial_x\Psi+\partial_x\Psi^*(H\Psi)\right]dx$; the kinetic terms cancel by parts, the potential terms give $\int\left[\Psi^*V\partial_x\Psi+\partial_x\Psi^*V\Psi\right]=-\int\Psi^*(\partial_xV)\Psi$.
steps.explain: Differentiate again: $\frac{d}{dt}\langle p\rangle$ with $\partial_t\Psi=\frac{1}{i\hbar}H\Psi$. The kinetic part of $H$ gives terms like $\Psi''^*\Psi'$, which integrate to zero by parts (they are total derivatives). The potential part gives $\int(\Psi^*V\Psi'+\Psi'^*V\Psi)=\int V\,\partial_x|\Psi|^2$; by parts this is $-\int V'|\Psi|^2$.

steps.reveal: $m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\langle x\rangle=-\langle\partial_xV\rangle$: Newton for averages. Not $-V^\prime(\langle x\rangle)$, except for at most quadratic $V$.
steps.explain: Reading the result: mass times the acceleration of the centre of the wave packet equals the average force. It is Newton's law for $\langle x\rangle$ only if $\langle V'(x)\rangle=V'(\langle x\rangle)$, which holds when $V'$ is linear, i.e. for free particles, constant forces and the harmonic oscillator.

enc.title: Sheet 2 Q2: Reality of energy

source.where: Exercise sheet II, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 2.pdf

enc.goal: Show that the expectation value of the Hamiltonian of a non-relativistic particle is real, $\langle H\rangle=\langle H\rangle^*$.

steps.reveal: $\langle H\rangle=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int\Psi^*\Psi^{\prime\prime}+\langle V\rangle$, $\langle H\rangle^*=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int\Psi^{*\prime\prime}\Psi+\langle V\rangle$ ($V$ real).
steps.explain: Take the complex conjugate of $\langle H\rangle=\int\Psi^*H\Psi$: $\Psi^*\leftrightarrow\Psi$ swap, and $V$ is real so $\langle V\rangle$ is unchanged. Only the kinetic term could differ: $\int\Psi^*\Psi''$ versus $\int\Psi^{*\prime\prime}\Psi$.

steps.reveal: $\int(\Psi^*\Psi^{\prime\prime}-\Psi^{*\prime\prime}\Psi)=\int(-\Psi^{*\prime}\Psi^\prime+\Psi^{*\prime}\Psi^\prime)=0$ by parts: $H$ is hermitian on normalisable states.
steps.explain: Integrate by parts once in each: both become $-\int\Psi^{*\prime}\Psi'$ (boundary terms vanish because $\Psi\to0$). Equal, so the difference is zero and $\langle H\rangle$ is real. This is the statement "$H$ is hermitian", and it is why energies are real.

enc.title: Sheet 2 Q3: Probability current

source.where: Exercise sheet II, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 2.pdf

enc.goal: Show that $\Psi_k=\left(Ae^{ikx/\hbar}+Be^{-ikx/\hbar}\right)e^{-iE_kt/\hbar}$, $E_k=k^2/2m$, solves the free Schrödinger equation and that its current is $j=\frac km(|A|^2-|B|^2)$.

steps.reveal: Each $e^{\pm ikx/\hbar}e^{-iE_kt/\hbar}$ solves it ($i\hbar\cdot(-iE_k/\hbar)=\frac{k^2}{2m}$), the time factor is even in $k$, and the equation is linear.
steps.explain: Here $k$ is a momentum (it is divided by $\hbar$). Check one plane wave: $\partial_x^2$ brings down $-k^2/\hbar^2$, so $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2\to\frac{k^2}{2m}$; $i\hbar\partial_t$ brings down $E_k$. Equal by definition of $E_k$. Both waves have the same $E_k$ (it depends on $k^2$), so their sum, with one common time factor, still solves the linear equation.

steps.reveal: $j=\frac{\hbar}{2mi}(\Psi^*\partial_x\Psi-\Psi\partial_x\Psi^*)$: the cross terms $AB^*$ cancel, leaving $\frac km(|A|^2-|B|^2)$: right-movers minus left-movers, each with velocity $k/m$ ($k$ is the momentum here).
steps.explain: Insert into $j$: $\partial_x\Psi$ multiplies $A$ by $\frac{ik}\hbar$ and $B$ by $-\frac{ik}\hbar$. In $\Psi^*\partial_x\Psi-\Psi\partial_x\Psi^*$ the mixed terms $AB^*$ and $A^*B$ appear twice with opposite signs and cancel; the pure terms give $\frac{2ik}{\hbar}(|A|^2-|B|^2)$. So the current is (velocity $k/m$) × (right-moving density minus left-moving density).

enc.title: Sheet 2 Q4: Probability current II

source.where: Exercise sheet II, Question 4; official solution: Solutions 2.pdf

enc.goal: At a fixed instant take the superposition of two right-moving plane waves $\Psi(x)=Ae^{ik_1x/\hbar}+Be^{ik_2x/\hbar}$ with $k_1,k_2>0$, $k_1\ne k_2$ ($k$ is a momentum here). Compute the probability current at $x=0$. Can it be left-moving, $j(0)<0$?

steps.reveal: $\Psi^\prime=\frac i\hbar\left(k_1Ae^{ik_1x/\hbar}+k_2Be^{ik_2x/\hbar}\right)$. In $j=\frac{\hbar}{2mi}(\Psi^*\Psi^\prime-\Psi\Psi^{*\prime})$ the diagonal terms now add (unlike $k_2=-k_1$ in Q3) and the cross terms carry $(k_1+k_2)$: $j(x)=\frac1m\left[k_1|A|^2+k_2|B|^2+(k_1+k_2)\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left(AB^*e^{i(k_1-k_2)x/\hbar}\right)\right]$.

$j(0)=\frac1m\left[k_1|A|^2+k_2|B|^2+(k_1+k_2)\,\mathrm{Re}(AB^*)\right]=\frac1{2m}\begin{pmatrix}A^*&B^*\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2k_1&k_1+k_2\\k_1+k_2&2k_2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A\\B\end{pmatrix}$, a hermitian quadratic form.

Its determinant is $4k_1k_2-(k_1+k_2)^2=-(k_1-k_2)^2<0$ and its trace $2(k_1+k_2)>0$: one positive and one negative eigenvalue. Choosing $(A,B)$ along the negative eigenvector gives $j(0)<0$: yes, the current can flow to the left although both waves move right. Example: $A=2$, $B=-1$ gives $j(0)=\frac{2k_1-k_2}m<0$ for $k_2>2k_1$. (This is quantum backflow; the current is only positive on average over $x$.)

keyPoints: $j(0)$ as a hermitian quadratic form in $(A,B)$

enc.title: Sheet 3 Q1: Gaussian wave functions

source.where: Exercise sheet III, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 3.pdf

enc.goal: $\Psi(x)=Ae^{-\lambda x^2/2}$, $\lambda>0$. (i) Normalise. (ii) Sketch; find $V$ (with $V(0)=0$) for which $\Psi$ is a stationary state, and $E$. (iii) Compute $\Delta x$, $\Delta p$ and $\Delta x\Delta p$. (iv) How would you tune $\lambda$ to localise the particle, and why can $\Delta x=0$ not be reached?

steps.reveal: $\int|A|^2e^{-\lambda x^2}dx=|A|^2\sqrt{\pi/\lambda}=1$: $A=(\lambda/\pi)^{1/4}$ (up to a phase).
steps.explain: Use the Gaussian integral $\int e^{-\lambda x^2}dx=\sqrt{\pi/\lambda}$ (worth knowing by heart). Setting $|A|^2\sqrt{\pi/\lambda}=1$ fixes $|A|$; the phase of $A$ is free because it is unobservable.

steps.reveal: $\Psi^{\prime\prime}=(\lambda^2x^2-\lambda)\Psi$, so $V=\frac{\hbar^2\lambda^2}{2m}x^2$ and $E=\frac{\hbar^2\lambda}{2m}$: the harmonic oscillator ground state ($\lambda=m\omega/\hbar$, $E=\hbar\omega/2$). Larger $\lambda$: narrower bell.
steps.explain: Run the Schrödinger equation backwards: differentiate $\Psi$ twice, $\Psi''=(\lambda^2x^2-\lambda)\Psi$, insert into $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Psi''+V\Psi=E\Psi$ and divide by $\Psi$. The $x^2$ part must be $V$, the constant part $E$ (with $V(0)=0$). A Gaussian is the ground state of a parabola, with $\lambda=m\omega/\hbar$.

steps.reveal: $\langle x\rangle=\langle p\rangle=0$, $\langle x^2\rangle=\frac1{2\lambda}$ (differentiate $\int e^{-\lambda x^2}$ w.r.t. $\lambda$), $\langle p^2\rangle=\frac{\hbar^2\lambda}2$: $\Delta x\Delta p=\frac\hbar2$, the minimum.
steps.explain:
Symmetry gives $\langle x\rangle=0$ (even $|\Psi|^2$ times odd $x$) and $\langle p\rangle=0$ (real $\Psi$).

The trick for $\langle x^2\rangle$: $\int x^2e^{-\lambda x^2}dx=-\frac{d}{d\lambda}\int e^{-\lambda x^2}dx$, which gives $\frac{1}{2\lambda}$ after normalising. $\langle p^2\rangle$$=\hbar^2\int|\Psi'|^2dx=\hbar^2\lambda^2\langle x^2\rangle$. The product $\frac{\hbar}{2}$ is the smallest Heisenberg allows: Gaussians are the minimum-uncertainty states.

steps.reveal: Large $\lambda$ (steep trap) gives small $\Delta x$, but $\Delta p=\hbar\sqrt{\lambda/2}$ and $E=\hbar^2\lambda/2m$ diverge: $\Delta x\to0$ costs infinite energy.
steps.explain: $\Delta x=1/\sqrt{2\lambda}$ shrinks as $\lambda$ grows, but $\Delta p\propto\sqrt\lambda$ and $E\propto\lambda$ grow. Squeezing a particle into a point needs an infinitely steep trap and infinite energy: localisation always costs kinetic energy.

enc.title: Sheet 3 Q2: Particle in a box I

source.where: Exercise sheet III, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 3.pdf

enc.goal: (i) A particle in $[0,a]$ has $\Psi(x,0)=1/\sqrt a$. Probability of measuring $E_n=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2ma^2}$? ($\psi_n=\sqrt{2/a}\sin\frac{n\pi x}a$.) (ii) Deduce $\sum_m\frac1{(2m-1)^2}=\frac{\pi^2}8$ and $\zeta(2)=\frac{\pi^2}6$.

steps.reveal: $p_n=\left|\int_0^a\sqrt{\frac2a}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{a}\frac{1}{\sqrt a}dx\right|^2=\frac{2}{n^2\pi^2}(1-(-1)^n)^2=\frac{8}{n^2\pi^2}$ for odd $n$, 0 for even $n$.
steps.explain: Measurement rule: expand the state in energy eigenstates; the probability of $E_n$ is $|c_n|^2$ with $c_n=\langle\psi_n|\Psi\rangle$. The integral of $\sin\frac{n\pi x}{a}$ over the box is $\frac{a}{n\pi}(1-\cos n\pi)=\frac{a}{n\pi}(1-(-1)^n)$: zero for even $n$ (the sine is antisymmetric about the middle, the constant state symmetric).

steps.reveal: $\sum p_n=1\Rightarrow\sum_{\rm odd}\frac1{n^2}=\frac{\pi^2}8$. Then $\zeta(2)=\frac{\zeta(2)}4+\frac{\pi^2}8$, so $\zeta(2)=\frac{\pi^2}6$.
steps.explain: Probabilities sum to 1. $\sum_{n\ \rm odd}\frac{8}{n^2\pi^2}=1$ gives the odd sum. For all $n$: split $\zeta(2)$ into even terms $\sum\frac1{(2m)^2}=\frac14\zeta(2)$ and odd terms $\frac{\pi^2}8$, and solve. Physics producing a famous maths identity.

enc.title: Sheet 3 Q3: Particle in a box II

source.where: Exercise sheet III, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 3.pdf

enc.goal: In the $n$-th eigenstate of the box $[0,a]$ show $\langle x\rangle=\frac a2$, $\langle(x-\langle x\rangle)^2\rangle=\frac{a^2}{12}\left(1-\frac{6}{n^2\pi^2}\right)$, and that the classical limit is approached as $n\to\infty$.

steps.reveal: $\langle x\rangle=\int_0^a\frac{x}{a}\left(1-\cos\frac{2\pi nx}a\right)dx=\frac a2$ (the cosine term integrates to 0 by parts).
steps.explain: $|\psi_n|^2=\frac2a\sin^2\frac{n\pi x}a=\frac1a\left(1-\cos\frac{2n\pi x}a\right)$ (double-angle formula). The constant part alone gives $a/2$; the cosine part integrates to zero against $x$ (by parts, or by symmetry about $a/2$). The probability density is symmetric about the middle, so the mean is the middle.

steps.reveal: $\langle x^2\rangle=\frac{a^2}3-\frac{a^2}{2\pi^2n^2}$ (two integrations by parts), so $(\Delta x)^2=\frac{a^2}{12}-\frac{a^2}{2\pi^2n^2}$.
steps.explain: $\langle x^2\rangle$: the constant part gives $a^2/3$; the cosine part needs two integrations by parts and gives $-\frac{a^2}{2\pi^2n^2}$. Then $(\Delta x)^2=\langle x^2\rangle-\langle x\rangle^2$.

steps.reveal: A classical particle is uniform on $[0,a]$: $\langle x\rangle=a/2$, $(\Delta x)^2=a^2/12$, reached for $n\to\infty$ (correspondence principle).
steps.explain: Classical comparison: a ball bouncing between walls spends equal time everywhere, so its position is uniformly distributed: mean $a/2$, variance $a^2/12$ (the variance of a uniform distribution). The quantum correction $\propto1/n^2$ disappears for highly excited states: correspondence principle.

keyPoints: uniform classical distribution as the limit

questions.title: Particle in a box III: the sudden wall

enc.title: Sheet 3 Q4: Particle in a box III: the sudden wall

source.where: Exercise sheet III, Question 4; official solution: Solutions 3.pdf

enc.goal: A particle in the ground state of $[0,a]$; the wall at $a$ jumps suddenly to $2a$. Expand in the eigenfunctions of $[0,2a]$, give $\Psi(x,t)$, show that only $n=2$ and odd $n$ contribute ($E_n=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{8ma^2}$) and that the energy is unchanged with probability 1/2. Classical intuition?

steps.reveal: $c_n=\frac{\sqrt2}{a}\int_0^a\sin\frac{\pi x}a\sin\frac{n\pi x}{2a}dx$; with $2\sin\sin=\cos-\cos$: $c_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}$, and for $n\ne2$: $c_n=\frac{\sin\pi(1-n/2)}{\sqrt2\pi(1-n/2)}-\frac{\sin\pi(1+n/2)}{\sqrt2\pi(1+n/2)}$, zero for even $n>2$.
steps.explain:
Sudden change: the wave function has no time to change, only the Hamiltonian does. So expand the old state in the eigenfunctions of the new box ($\frac1{\sqrt a}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{2a}$ on $[0,2a]$), integrating only over $[0,a]$ where the old state lives.

The integral: $\sin A\sin B=\frac12[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)]$ turns it into cosine integrals. For $n=2$ the two sines are the same function: $c_2=\frac{\sqrt2}{a}\cdot\frac a2$. For even $n>2$ both terms contain $\sin(\text{integer}\cdot\pi)=0$.

steps.reveal: $\Psi(x,t)=\sum c_n\psi_n(x)e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}$. $E_2$ of the new box equals the old ground energy: probability $|c_2|^2=\frac12$ (odd $n$: $P_n=\frac{32}{\pi^2(4-n^2)^2}$).
steps.explain: Each new eigenstate evolves with its own phase $e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}$. The new $n=2$ level has $E_2=\frac{4\pi^2\hbar^2}{8ma^2}$, exactly the old ground energy (twice the box, twice the wavelength fits as the second harmonic). So "energy unchanged" means "found in $n=2$", probability $|c_2|^2=\frac12$.

steps.reveal: The particle bounces freely; moving a wall instantly (not touching it) does not change its kinetic energy. Quantum mechanically the mean energy is conserved too ($\langle H\rangle$ of the unchanged state), but individual outcomes spread.
steps.explain: Classically nothing touches the particle when the wall jumps away, so its energy cannot change. Quantum mechanically the average energy is unchanged too (same state, and $H$ inside $[0,a]$ is the same), but a single measurement can give other levels.

enc.title: Sheet 4 Q1: One-dimensional delta potential

source.where: Exercise sheet IV, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 4.pdf

enc.goal: $V=V\delta(x)$; ansatz $\psi=e^{ikx/\hbar}+Re^{-ikx/\hbar}$ ($x<0$), $Te^{ikx/\hbar}$ ($x>0$), $E=k^2/2m$. Find the matching conditions, $R$, $T$ and check $|R|^2+|T|^2=1$.

steps.reveal: Integrate from $-\epsilon$ to $\epsilon$: $\psi$ continuous, $\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(\psi^\prime(0^+)-\psi^\prime(0^-))=V\psi(0)$.
steps.explain: Why integrate across the delta. At $x=0$ the potential is infinite, so $\psi''$ has a delta there too, i.e. $\psi'$ jumps. Integrate the Schrödinger equation from $-\epsilon$ to $\epsilon$: $\int\psi''=\psi'(0^+)-\psi'(0^-)$, $\int E\psi\to0$, $\int V\delta\psi=V\psi(0)$. $\psi$ itself stays continuous (a jump in $\psi$ would need a $\delta'$).

steps.reveal: $1+R=T$ and $\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{ik}{\hbar}(T-1+R)=VT$ give $R=\frac{-imV}{\hbar k+imV}$, $T=\frac{\hbar k}{\hbar k+imV}$.
steps.explain: Two conditions, two unknowns. Continuity: $1+R=T$. Jump: with $\psi'=\frac{ik}\hbar(\dots)$ on both sides, $\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{ik}{\hbar}(T-1+R)=VT$. Insert $T=1+R$ and solve for $R$; then $T=1+R$.

steps.reveal: $|R|^2+|T|^2=\frac{m^2V^2+\hbar^2k^2}{\hbar^2k^2+m^2V^2}=1$. High energies transmit, the sign of $V$ does not matter for $|T|$.
steps.explain: $|R|^2=\frac{m^2V^2}{\hbar^2k^2+m^2V^2}$, $|T|^2=\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{\hbar^2k^2+m^2V^2}$: they add to 1 (particles are neither created nor lost, sheet 4 Q3). Fast particles ($k$ large) barely notice the spike. $V$ enters only as $V^2$: a delta wall and a delta well reflect equally.

enc.title: Sheet 4 Q2: Infinitely deep, infinitely narrow well

source.where: Exercise sheet IV, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 4.pdf

enc.goal: Square well $V=-V_0$ for $|x|<a$. Show that for $V_0\to\infty$, $a\to0$ with $V_0a$ fixed the ground-state energy stays finite and negative.

steps.reveal: $\psi=b\cos kx$ inside, $e^{-\kappa|x|}$ outside, $k=\sqrt{2m(E+V_0)}/\hbar$, $\kappa=\sqrt{-2mE}/\hbar$; matching: $e^{-\kappa a}=b\cos ka$, $\kappa e^{-\kappa a}=bk\sin ka$.
steps.explain: Ground state is even (no node), so inside take $\cos kx$ and outside the decaying exponential. Match $\psi$ and $\psi'$ at $x=a$ (the other side follows by symmetry).

steps.reveal: $ka\to0$ (since $k\sim\sqrt{V_0}$, $a\sim1/V_0$): $b=1$, $\kappa=k^2a\to\frac{2mV_0a}{\hbar^2}$, so $E_0=-\frac{\hbar^2\kappa^2}{2m}=-\frac{2m(V_0a)^2}{\hbar^2}$, finite.
steps.explain: The limit. Divide the two matching equations: $\kappa=k\tan ka$. As $V_0\to\infty$ with $V_0a$ fixed, $k\approx\sqrt{2mV_0}/\hbar$ grows like $\sqrt{V_0}$ but $a$ shrinks like $1/V_0$, so $ka\to0$ and $\tan ka\approx ka$: $\kappa=k^2a=\frac{2mV_0a}{\hbar^2}$, finite. The energy $-\hbar^2\kappa^2/2m$ is finite and negative.

steps.reveal: The well becomes $-2V_0a\,\delta(x)$; with the jump condition of Q1, $\psi=e^{-\kappa|x|}$ gives the same $\kappa$. Exactly one bound state.
steps.explain: Why this is a delta. A deep narrow well with fixed area $\int V\,dx=-2V_0a$ is what a delta function is. Using the jump condition of Q1 with strength $-2V_0a$ gives the same $\kappa$ in one line. One bound state, as for every attractive delta.

enc.title: Sheet 4 Q3: General potentials

source.where: Exercise sheet IV, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 4.pdf

enc.goal: (i) For a stationary scattering state $\chi=e^{ikx}+Ae^{-ikx}$ ($x\ll0$), $Be^{ikx}$ ($x\gg0$) show that $j$ is independent of $x$ and $|A|^2+|B|^2=1$; interpret. (ii) Show $\langle T\rangle\ge0$ and that the lowest energy in any well lies above the bottom of the well.

steps.reveal: $\partial_xj=-\partial_t|\psi|^2=0$ for stationary states. Left: $j=\frac{\hbar k}m(1-|A|^2)$, right: $\frac{\hbar k}m|B|^2$: equal, so $|A|^2+|B|^2=1$: every particle is reflected or transmitted.
steps.explain: Continuity equation: $\partial_t|\psi|^2+\partial_xj=0$. A stationary state has $|\psi|^2$ independent of time, so $\partial_xj=0$: the current is the same everywhere. Evaluate it far left (incoming minus reflected, sheet 2 Q3) and far right (transmitted) and set them equal: reflection plus transmission probability is 1.

steps.reveal: $\langle T\rangle=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int|\partial_x\psi|^2\ge0$ (by parts), strictly $>0$ for a normalisable state. Hence $\langle H\rangle\ge V_{\min}+\langle T\rangle>V_{\min}$.
steps.explain: Kinetic energy is positive: $\langle T\rangle=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int\psi^*\psi''$, and one integration by parts gives $\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int|\psi'|^2\ge0$; zero only for a constant, which is not normalisable. Since $\langle V\rangle\ge V_{\min}$, every state, the ground state included, has energy strictly above the bottom of the well: the particle can never just sit at the minimum.

enc.title: Sheet 4 Q4: The deuteron

source.where: Exercise sheet IV, Question 4; official solution: Solutions 4.pdf

enc.goal: 3D square well $V=-V$ for $r<a$, 0 outside. Find the spherically symmetric bound states (hint: $\chi=r\psi$). Is there always a bound state?

steps.reveal: $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\chi^{\prime\prime}+V(r)\chi=E\chi$ with $\chi(0)=0$: the 1D well, but only odd solutions.
steps.explain: Why $\chi=r\psi$. For a spherically symmetric $\psi(r)$, $\nabla^2\psi=\frac1r\frac{d^2}{dr^2}(r\psi)$. So with $\chi=r\psi$ the 3D equation becomes the 1D Schrödinger equation for $\chi$ on $r>0$. And $\psi$ must stay finite at the origin, so $\chi(0)=0$: like a 1D well with a hard wall at the centre, i.e. only the odd 1D solutions survive.

steps.reveal: $\chi=\sin kr$ inside, $e^{-\kappa r}$ outside; with $\xi=ka$, $\eta=\kappa a$: $\eta=-\xi\cot\xi$ and $\xi^2+\eta^2=\frac{2ma^2V}{\hbar^2}$.
steps.explain: Inside: $\chi=\sin kr$ (vanishes at 0). Outside: $e^{-\kappa r}$. Matching $\chi'/\chi$ at $r=a$: $k\cot ka=-\kappa$. In dimensionless form $\eta=-\xi\cot\xi$, and $\xi^2+\eta^2$ is fixed by the depth ($k^2+\kappa^2=2mV/\hbar^2$): a circle in the $(\xi,\eta)$ plane.

steps.reveal: $-\xi\cot\xi<0$ for $\xi<\pi/2$, so a solution needs $\frac{2ma^2V}{\hbar^2}>\frac{\pi^2}4$: unlike 1D, a 3D well needs a minimum depth $V>\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{8ma^2}$. The deuteron is barely bound.
steps.explain: Graphical solution: we need $\eta>0$, but $-\xi\cot\xi$ is negative until $\xi=\pi/2$. So the circle must have radius $>\pi/2$: a minimum depth. In 1D an even ground state exists for any depth; in 3D the wall at $r=0$ (the odd condition) removes it. The deuteron is just above this threshold, so it has a single, weakly bound state.

enc.title: Sheet 5 Q1: Transfer matrix method

source.where: Exercise sheet V, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 5.pdf

enc.goal: Piecewise constant potentials. (i) Step $V_L\to V_R$ at 0: find $M$ with $\binom{A_L}{B_L}=M\binom{A_R}{B_R}$. (ii) Propagation matrix $N$ over a region $[x_1,x_2]$. (iii) Chain them for a general potential. (iv) Square well $-V$ for $|x|<\ell/2$: $M_{\rm full}$; when is $N=I$, and what does it mean? (v) Barrier $V$, $0<E<V$, $B_R=0$, $A_L=1$: show $|B_L|^2+|A_R|^2=1$ and compute $|A_R|^2$.

steps.reveal: Continuity of $\psi,\psi^\prime$: $A_L+B_L=A_R+B_R$, $k(A_L-B_L)=q(A_R-B_R)$, so $M=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1+\eta&1-\eta\\1-\eta&1+\eta\end{pmatrix}$, $\eta=q/k$.
steps.explain: Idea of transfer matrices: in each region with constant $V$ the solution is $Ae^{ikx}+Be^{-ikx}$, i.e. just two numbers. At a step, continuity of $\psi$ and $\psi'$ gives two linear equations linking the left pair $(A_L,B_L)$ to the right pair $(A_R,B_R)$: a $2\times2$ matrix. Add and subtract the two equations to solve for $A_L$ and $B_L$.

steps.reveal: $N=\mathrm{diag}(e^{-ik\ell},e^{ik\ell})$, $\ell=x_2-x_1$. In general $\binom{A_L}{B_L}=M_{n+1,n}N_nM_{n,n-1}\cdots N_1M_{1,0}\binom{A_R}{B_R}$.
steps.explain: Propagation: moving the reference point by $\ell$ multiplies $e^{\pm ikx}$ by $e^{\pm ik\ell}$: a diagonal matrix. Any potential built from steps is then a product of step and propagation matrices, read from right to left, like optics with lenses.

steps.reveal: $M_{\rm full}=M^{-1}NM$ with $q=\sqrt{2m(E+V)}/\hbar$. $N=I$ iff $q\ell=2\pi n$: the wave fits into the well, $M_{\rm full}=I$, perfect transmission (resonance).
steps.explain: Resonance: if $q\ell$ is a multiple of $2\pi$, the wave inside comes out with the same phase it went in, $N=I$, and the two step matrices cancel ($M^{-1}M=I$): the well becomes invisible, transmission is perfect. Same physics as a Fabry–Pérot interferometer or the Ramsauer effect.

steps.reveal: $q=i\kappa$, $\alpha=k/\kappa$: $1=A_R(\cosh\kappa\ell+\frac i2\frac{1-\alpha^2}{\alpha}\sinh\kappa\ell)$, $B_L=A_R\frac i2\frac{1+\alpha^2}\alpha\sinh\kappa\ell$; squaring gives $|A_R|^2+|B_L|^2=1$ and $T=|A_R|^2=\left[1+\frac{V^2}{4E(V-E)}\sinh^2\kappa\ell\right]^{-1}$. Classically $T=0$.
steps.explain: Below the barrier the inside wave number is imaginary, $q=i\kappa$, and $e^{\pm iq x}$ become growing and decaying exponentials; cosh and sinh appear instead of cos and sin. Square $|A_R|$ to get $T$. For a thick barrier $\sinh\kappa\ell\approx\frac12e^{\kappa\ell}$, so $T\propto e^{-2\kappa\ell}$: tunnelling.

enc.title: Sheet 5 Q2: Rays in $\mathbb C^2$

source.where: Exercise sheet V, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 5.pdf

enc.goal: $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^2$ with basis $|1\rangle,|2\rangle$. (i) Are $|\Psi\rangle$ and $\mu|\Psi\rangle$ physically different? (ii) Show almost every state is $|1\rangle+z|2\rangle$; which are not, and do different $z$ give different states? (iii) What state is $|z|\to\infty$? (iv) What geometric object is the space of states?

steps.reveal: All probabilities $\frac{|\langle\Phi|\Psi\rangle|^2}{\langle\Phi|\Phi\rangle\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}$ are unchanged by $\mu$: physical states are rays.
steps.explain: Every probability formula is homogeneous: numerator and denominator both contain $|\mu|^2$. So $\mu|\Psi\rangle$ predicts exactly the same as $|\Psi\rangle$: a physical state is a whole line (ray) of vectors, not one vector.

steps.reveal: $a|1\rangle+b|2\rangle\sim|1\rangle+\frac ba|2\rangle$ if $a\ne0$; distinct $z$ are distinct rays. Only $|2\rangle$ is missing, and it is the limit $|z|\to\infty$.
steps.explain: Choosing a representative: if $a\ne0$, divide by $a$: every ray with $a\ne0$ contains exactly one vector of the form $|1\rangle+z|2\rangle$, and $z=b/a$ labels it uniquely. The only ray missed has $a=0$: $|2\rangle$, reached as $z\to\infty$.

steps.reveal: $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$ is the Riemann sphere $S^2$ (stereographic projection): the Bloch sphere of a spin-$\frac12$/qubit, $\mathbb{CP}^1\cong S^2$.
steps.explain: The complex plane plus one point at infinity is a sphere (stereographic projection). So the states of any two-level system form a sphere: the Bloch sphere, with $|1\rangle$ and $|2\rangle$ at the poles.

enc.title: Sheet 5 Q3: Commutators

source.where: Exercise sheet V, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 5.pdf

enc.goal: (i) Show $(iAB)^\dagger=-iB^\dagger A^\dagger$ and that $i[A,B]$ is self-adjoint for self-adjoint $A,B$. (ii) With $[x,p]=i\hbar$ show $e^{iap/\hbar}xe^{-iap/\hbar}=x+a$. (iii) Deduce $e^{iap/\hbar}f(x)e^{-iap/\hbar}=f(x+a)$ and Weyl’s relation $e^{iap/\hbar}e^{ibx/\hbar}=e^{iba/\hbar}e^{ibx/\hbar}e^{iap/\hbar}$.

steps.reveal: $\langle f|iABg\rangle=\langle-iB^\dagger A^\dagger f|g\rangle$ for all $f,g$. Then $(i[A,B])^\dagger=-iBA+iAB=i[A,B]$.
steps.explain: Adjoint of a product: move operators to the other side of the scalar product one by one, reversing the order; the $i$ becomes $-i$. For the commutator, $(i[A,B])^\dagger=-i(B^\dagger A^\dagger-A^\dagger B^\dagger)=-i(BA-AB)=i[A,B]$: hermitian. That is why $[x,p]=i\hbar$ needs the $i$.

steps.reveal: $p^nx=xp^n-ni\hbar p^{n-1}$, so $e^{iap/\hbar}x=(x+a)e^{iap/\hbar}$; multiply by $e^{-iap/\hbar}$ from the right ($e^{iap/\hbar}e^{-iap/\hbar}=I$).
steps.explain: Move $x$ through powers of $p$: $[p,x]=-i\hbar$, so each time $x$ passes one $p$ it leaves $-i\hbar$ behind; for $p^n$ that happens $n$ times. In the exponential series this produces $x\,e^{iap/\hbar}+a\,e^{iap/\hbar}$. So $e^{iap/\hbar}$ shifts $x$ by $a$: momentum generates translations.

steps.reveal: Conjugation is multiplicative, so $x^n\to(x+a)^n$ and $f(x)\to f(x+a)$. With $f=e^{ibx/\hbar}$: $e^{iap/\hbar}e^{ibx/\hbar}=e^{ib(x+a)/\hbar}e^{iap/\hbar}$, the Weyl form.
steps.explain: Conjugation respects products: $Ux^2U^{-1}=(UxU^{-1})(UxU^{-1})$. So every power and every power series in $x$ is shifted: $f(x)\to f(x+a)$. Taking $f=e^{ibx/\hbar}$ gives an extra phase $e^{iba/\hbar}$ when the two exponentials are swapped: Weyl's form of $[x,p]=i\hbar$.

enc.title: Sheet 6 Q1: Delta well in momentum space

source.where: Exercise sheet VI, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 6.pdf

enc.goal: $V=-\alpha\delta(x)$. (i) Bound states in position space. (ii) Show the momentum-space equation $\frac{p^2}{2m}\tilde\psi+\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\int\tilde V(p-p^\prime)\tilde\psi(p^\prime)dp^\prime=E\tilde\psi$. (iii) Compute $\tilde V$ and solve in terms of $C=\int\tilde\psi\,dp$. (iv) Get the allowed $E$. (v) Compare with the Fourier transform of (i). (vi) What goes wrong for $E>0$, or for a barrier?

steps.reveal: $\psi=Ae^{-\kappa|x|}$, jump $\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(\psi^\prime(0^+)-\psi^\prime(0^-))=-\alpha\psi(0)$ gives $\kappa=\frac{m\alpha}{\hbar^2}$, one bound state $E=-\frac{m\alpha^2}{2\hbar^2}$.
steps.explain: Same as sheet 4 Q1/Q2: away from 0 the solution decays like $e^{-\kappa|x|}$; the jump in $\psi'$ is $-2\kappa\psi(0)$, and the delta demands $-\frac{2m\alpha}{\hbar^2}\psi(0)$. So $\kappa=m\alpha/\hbar^2$ and one bound state.

steps.reveal: Fourier transforming, $V\psi$ becomes a convolution; $\tilde V=-\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}$ is constant, so the integral term is $-\frac{\alpha C}{2\pi\hbar}$ and $\left(\frac{p^2}{2m}-E\right)\tilde\psi=\frac{\alpha C}{2\pi\hbar}$: $\tilde\psi(p)=\frac{\alpha C}{2\pi\hbar}\,\frac{1}{p^2/2m-E}$, with $C=\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}\,\psi(0)$.
steps.explain: Fourier transforming the equation: $p^2/2m$ becomes multiplication, and a product $V(x)\psi(x)$ becomes a convolution of the transforms. A delta in $x$ has a constant transform, so the convolution is just a constant times $\int\tilde\psi\,dp=C$. Then the equation is algebraic: $(p^2/2m-E)\tilde\psi=$ const, solved by division.

steps.reveal: Integrating both sides: $C=\frac{m\alpha C}{\hbar\sqrt{-2mE}}$, so $\hbar\sqrt{-2mE}=m\alpha$: the same $E$. The transform of $e^{-\kappa|x|}$ is a Lorentzian $\propto\frac{2\kappa}{\kappa^2+p^2/\hbar^2}$: the same function.
steps.explain: Self-consistency: $C$ is defined as $\int\tilde\psi\,dp$, and $\tilde\psi$ contains $C$. Integrate the solution over $p$ ($\int\frac{dp}{p^2+2m|E|}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2m|E|}}$): $C$ cancels and an equation for $E$ remains, the same $E$ as in position space. The shape $\frac1{p^2+\hbar^2\kappa^2}$ (a Lorentzian) is indeed the Fourier transform of $e^{-\kappa|x|}$.

steps.reveal: $E>0$: poles at $p=\pm\sqrt{2mE}$, $C$ diverges (scattering states are not normalisable). Barrier $+\alpha^\prime\delta$: $-m\alpha^\prime=\hbar\sqrt{-2mE}>0$ is impossible: no bound state.
steps.explain: For $E>0$ the denominator $p^2/2m-E$ vanishes at real $p$ and the integral diverges: scattering states are not normalisable, so there is no bound state there. For a repulsive delta the condition would need $\sqrt{-2mE}<0$, which is impossible: a barrier binds nothing.

enc.title: Sheet 6 Q2: Uncertainty relation in a box

source.where: Exercise sheet VI, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 6.pdf

enc.goal: For the $n$-th eigenstate of the box $[0,a]$ ($\langle x\rangle=a/2$, $(\Delta x)^2=\frac{a^2}{12}(1-\frac6{n^2\pi^2})$, sheet III) compute $\langle p\rangle$, $\Delta p$ and check $\Delta x\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$.

steps.reveal: $\langle p\rangle=0$ (the integrand $\sin\cos$ is odd about $a/2$), $\langle p^2\rangle=\left(\frac{n\pi\hbar}a\right)^2$ (also $=2mE_n$), so $\Delta p=\frac{n\pi\hbar}a$.
steps.explain: $\langle p\rangle=-i\hbar\int\psi\psi'$: the integrand $\sin\cos$ is antisymmetric about the middle, so 0 (a real stationary state does not move). $\langle p^2\rangle=2m\langle T\rangle=2mE_n$ since inside the box $V=0$: $\left(\frac{n\pi\hbar}{a}\right)^2$.

steps.reveal: $\Delta x\Delta p=\frac\hbar2\sqrt{\frac{n^2\pi^2}3-2}\ge\frac\hbar2\times1.13$ for $n=1$, growing with $n$: Heisenberg holds, not saturated.
steps.explain: Multiply $\Delta x$ from sheet 3 Q3 with $\Delta p$: $\frac\hbar2\sqrt{\frac{n^2\pi^2}{3}-2}$. Already for $n=1$ the root is $1.13>1$, so Heisenberg holds but is not saturated (the box state is not a Gaussian).

enc.title: Sheet 6 Q3: Uncertainty relation and energy

source.where: Exercise sheet VI, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 6.pdf

enc.goal: $V=\frac12kx^2$. Express $\langle E\rangle$ through $\langle x\rangle,\langle p\rangle,\Delta x,\Delta p$, and use $\Delta x\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$ to show $\langle E\rangle\ge\frac\hbar2\sqrt{k/m}$.

steps.reveal: $\langle E\rangle=\frac{(\Delta p)^2+\langle p\rangle^2}{2m}+\frac k2\left((\Delta x)^2+\langle x\rangle^2\right)\ge\frac{(\Delta p)^2}{2m}+\frac k2(\Delta x)^2$.
steps.explain: Rewrite with variances: $\langle p^2\rangle=(\Delta p)^2+\langle p\rangle^2$ (definition of variance), the same for $x$. Dropping the squares of the means can only lower the value, hence "$\ge$".

steps.reveal: Complete the square: $\ge\sqrt{k/m}\,\Delta x\Delta p\ge\frac\hbar2\sqrt{k/m}=\frac{\hbar\omega}2$ (or minimise $\frac{\mu}{2m}+\frac{k\hbar^2}{8\mu}$ over $\mu=(\Delta p)^2$). The zero-point energy is forced by uncertainty, and it is exactly the true ground state.
steps.explain: AM–GM inequality $u+v\ge2\sqrt{uv}$ with $u=\frac{(\Delta p)^2}{2m}$, $v=\frac k2(\Delta x)^2$: $\ge\sqrt{k/m}\,\Delta x\Delta p$, then Heisenberg. Small $\Delta x$ forces large $\Delta p$ and vice versa; the best compromise costs $\frac12\hbar\omega$. The oscillator ground state saturates every step, so this bound is the exact ground energy.

keyPoints: expectation values split into mean$^2$ + variance

questions.title: Free electron in a magnetic field

enc.title: Sheet 7 Q1: Free electron in a magnetic field

source.where: Exercise sheet VII (HS26), Question 1 (new this year); official solution: sheet_7_solutions.pdf, (S.1)–(S.8)

enc.goal: An electron (mass $m$, charge $-e$, $e>0$) moves in the $xy$ plane in a homogeneous field $B\hat z$: $H=\frac1{2m}\left(\vec p+\frac ec\vec A\right)^2$ (Gaussian units), Landau gauge $\vec A=(0,Bx)$. (i) Separate variables and map the problem to a harmonic oscillator; with $\omega_c=\frac{eB}{mc}$ and the magnetic length $\ell=\sqrt{\hbar c/eB}$, find the energies and eigenfunctions in terms of the 1D oscillator eigenfunctions $\chi_n$. (ii) Add a homogeneous electric field along $x$, potential $\phi(x)=-\mathcal Ex$. How does the spectrum change?

steps.reveal: $H=\frac1{2m}\left(p_x^2+\left(p_y+\frac{eB}cx\right)^2\right)$ does not contain $y$, so $[p_y,H]=0$: take $\psi=\chi(x)e^{ik_yy}$ ($k_y$ a wave number). Then $\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2+\frac m2\omega_c^2\left(x+k_y\ell^2\right)^2\right)\chi=E\chi$, using $\frac{eB}c=m\omega_c$ and $\hbar=m\omega_c\ell^2$.

A harmonic oscillator of frequency $\omega_c$ centred at $x_0=-k_y\ell^2$: $E_n=\hbar\omega_c\left(n+\frac12\right)$, $\psi_{n,k_y}(x,y)=e^{ik_yy}\chi_n(x+k_y\ell^2)$. $E_n$ does not depend on $k_y$: every level is degenerate, with one state per allowed $k_y$ (infinitely many on the infinite plane).

The charge $-e$ in $\phi=-\mathcal Ex$ has potential energy $+e\mathcal Ex$; $H$ still does not contain $y$. Completing the square: $\frac m2\omega_c^2(x+k_y\ell^2)^2+e\mathcal Ex=\frac m2\omega_c^2\left(x+k_y\ell^2+\frac{e\mathcal E}{m\omega_c^2}\right)^2-\hbar k_y\frac{\mathcal Ec}B-\frac m2\frac{\mathcal E^2c^2}{B^2}$: a shifted oscillator. $E_{n,k_y}=\hbar\omega_c\left(n+\frac12\right)-\hbar k_y\frac{\mathcal Ec}B-\frac m2\frac{\mathcal E^2c^2}{B^2}$: the spacing $\hbar\omega_c$ stays, the degeneracy in $k_y$ is lifted (the energy now depends on where the orbit sits, $x_0$, through the potential; $\mathcal Ec/B$ is the drift velocity).

keyPoints: electric field: complete the square, $E$ gains $-\hbar k_y\mathcal Ec/B-\frac m2\mathcal E^2c^2/B^2$

enc.title: Sheet 7 Q2: 2D harmonic oscillator

source.where: Exercise sheet VII, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 7.pdf

enc.goal: $H=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\left(-\partial_x^2-\partial_y^2+x^2+y^2\right)$ (dimensionless coordinates). (i) Introduce $a,a^\dagger,b,b^\dagger$ and show $H=\hbar\omega(a^\dagger a+b^\dagger b+1)$; give their commutators. (ii) Find the eigenstates and the vacuum wave function $\psi_0(x,y)$. (iii) Show that $H$ is invariant under $\binom{a}{b}\to R(\varphi)\binom{a}{b}$, $R=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\varphi&-\sin\varphi\\ \sin\varphi&\cos\varphi\end{pmatrix}$ (same on $a^\dagger,b^\dagger$); what does it do to $x,y$? (iv) Find the generator $J$: $[J,a]=\frac{d}{d\varphi}a(\varphi)|_0$, $[J,b]=\frac{d}{d\varphi}b(\varphi)|_0$. (v) Show $[H,J]=0$ and diagonalise $J$ on the states with $E\le2\hbar\omega$.

steps.reveal: $a=\frac1{\sqrt2}(x+\partial_x)$, $a^\dagger=\frac1{\sqrt2}(x-\partial_x)$, same for $b$ with $y$. $[a,a^\dagger]=[b,b^\dagger]=1$, all other commutators vanish. $a^\dagger a=\frac12(x^2-1-\partial_x^2)$, hence $H=\hbar\omega(a^\dagger a+b^\dagger b+1)$.
steps.explain:
Why it separates: $H$ is a sum of an $x$ part and a $y$ part, each a 1D oscillator. So build ladder operators for each separately; operators for different coordinates commute.

Check $a^\dagger a$: $\frac12(x-\partial_x)(x+\partial_x)=\frac12(x^2+x\partial_x-\partial_xx-\partial_x^2)$, and $\partial_x x-x\partial_x=1$ (product rule), so $a^\dagger a=\frac12(x^2-\partial_x^2-1)$. Adding both coordinates: $H=\hbar\omega(a^\dagger a+\frac12+b^\dagger b+\frac12)$.

steps.reveal: $|m,n\rangle=\frac{(a^\dagger)^m(b^\dagger)^n}{\sqrt{m!\,n!}}|0,0\rangle$, $E=\hbar\omega(m+n+1)$ (degeneracy $N+1$ at $E=\hbar\omega(N+1)$). $a|0\rangle=b|0\rangle=0$ gives $(x+\partial_x)\psi_0=(y+\partial_y)\psi_0=0$: $\psi_0=\pi^{-1/2}e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}$.
steps.explain: Eigenstates are products: $m$ quanta in $x$ and $n$ in $y$. The energy depends only on $m+n=N$, and there are $N+1$ ways to split $N$: degeneracy $N+1$. The vacuum is killed by $a$ and $b$, two first-order equations whose solution is the Gaussian.

steps.reveal: $H=\hbar\omega\,(a^\dagger\ b^\dagger)\binom ab+\hbar\omega$ and $R^TR=I$, so $H$ is invariant. Since $x=(a+a^\dagger)/\sqrt2$, $y=(b+b^\dagger)/\sqrt2$, $x,y$ are rotated by the same $R(\varphi)$: rotational symmetry of the isotropic oscillator.
steps.explain: Invariance: $H$ contains $a^\dagger a+b^\dagger b$, the "length squared" of the vector $(a,b)$. A rotation (real orthogonal, $R^TR=I$) keeps length. Since $x\propto a+a^\dagger$ and $y\propto b+b^\dagger$, rotating $(a,b)$ rotates $(x,y)$ by the same angle: the symmetry is ordinary rotation of the plane.

steps.reveal: $\frac{d}{d\varphi}a(\varphi)|_0=-b$, $\frac{d}{d\varphi}b(\varphi)|_0=a$; $J=a^\dagger b-b^\dagger a$ does it ($[a^\dagger b,a]=-b$, $[-b^\dagger a,b]=a$). $iJ$ is (up to $\hbar$) the angular momentum $L_z$.
steps.explain: Generator = the derivative of the transformation at $\varphi=0$: $a\to a-\varphi b$, $b\to b+\varphi a$. We need an operator whose commutators reproduce this. Try $J=a^\dagger b-b^\dagger a$ and use $[a^\dagger,a]=-1$: $[J,a]=-b$, $[J,b]=a$. Up to $i\hbar$ it is $L_z$.

steps.reveal: $[H,a^\dagger b]=a^\dagger(-\hbar\omega b)+\hbar\omega a^\dagger b=0$, same for $b^\dagger a$. $J|m,n\rangle=\sqrt{(m+1)n}|m+1,n-1\rangle-\sqrt{m(n+1)}|m-1,n+1\rangle$. On $\{|0,0\rangle,|1,0\rangle,|0,1\rangle\}$: $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, eigenvectors $|0,0\rangle$ (0), $\frac1{\sqrt2}(|1,0\rangle\pm i|0,1\rangle)$ ($\pm i$).
steps.explain: $[H,J]=0$: $a^\dagger b$ removes a quantum from $y$ and adds one to $x$, so it does not change $N$, hence not $E$. A conserved operator can be diagonalised inside each energy level. On the level $N=1$ ($|1,0\rangle,|0,1\rangle$) $J$ is a $2\times2$ antisymmetric matrix with eigenvalues $\pm i$: the combinations $|1,0\rangle\pm i|0,1\rangle$, which are $x\pm iy$ states, i.e. angular momentum $\pm\hbar$.

enc.title: Sheet 7 Q3: Coherent states

source.where: Exercise sheet VII, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 7.pdf

enc.goal: $a|\alpha\rangle=\alpha|\alpha\rangle$, $\langle\alpha|\alpha\rangle=1$. (i) Show $|\alpha\rangle=e^{-|\alpha|^2/2}e^{\alpha a^\dagger}|0\rangle$. (ii) Show $|\alpha\rangle(t)=e^{-i\omega t/2}|\alpha e^{-i\omega t}\rangle$. (iii) Compute $\langle x\rangle(t)$, $\langle p\rangle(t)$ and compare with the classical motion. (iv) Show $\Delta x\Delta p=\hbar/2$. (v) Show completeness $\int\frac{d\alpha^*d\alpha}{2\pi i}|\alpha\rangle\langle\alpha|=I$. (vi) Show that $\langle x|\alpha\rangle$ is a Gaussian.

steps.reveal: $a\sum c_n|n\rangle=\sum c_{n+1}\sqrt{n+1}|n\rangle=\alpha\sum c_n|n\rangle$ gives $c_n=\frac{\alpha^n}{\sqrt{n!}}c_0$, i.e. $|\alpha\rangle=c_0e^{\alpha a^\dagger}|0\rangle$; normalisation $|c_0|^2e^{|\alpha|^2}=1$.
steps.explain: Expand in number states $|\alpha\rangle=\sum c_n|n\rangle$. $a$ lowers: $a|n\rangle=\sqrt n|n-1\rangle$. Comparing coefficients of $|n\rangle$ in $a|\alpha\rangle=\alpha|\alpha\rangle$ gives $c_{n+1}\sqrt{n+1}=\alpha c_n$, so $c_n=\frac{\alpha^n}{\sqrt{n!}}c_0$. And $\frac{\alpha^n}{\sqrt{n!}}|n\rangle=\frac{(\alpha a^\dagger)^n}{n!}|0\rangle$: the sum is an exponential. Normalisation: $\sum\frac{|\alpha|^{2n}}{n!}=e^{|\alpha|^2}$.

steps.reveal: $e^{-iHt/\hbar}|n\rangle=e^{-i\omega(n+\frac12)t}|n\rangle$, so $\alpha^n\to(\alpha e^{-i\omega t})^n$ and a global $e^{-i\omega t/2}$: again coherent with $\alpha(t)=\alpha e^{-i\omega t}$.
steps.explain: Each $|n\rangle$ picks up $e^{-i\omega(n+\frac12)t}$. The $n$-dependent part combines with $\alpha^n$ into $(\alpha e^{-i\omega t})^n$; the $\frac12$ is a common phase. So a coherent state stays coherent, with $\alpha$ turning in the complex plane at frequency $\omega$.

steps.reveal: $x=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}}(a+a^\dagger)$, $p=-i\sqrt{\frac{m\hbar\omega}2}(a-a^\dagger)$: $\langle x\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{2\hbar}{m\omega}}|\alpha|\cos(\omega t-\phi_0)$, $\langle p\rangle=-\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}|\alpha|\sin(\omega t-\phi_0)$: the classical oscillation (Ehrenfest is exact for the oscillator, $\langle V^\prime(x)\rangle=V^\prime(\langle x\rangle)$).
steps.explain: Write $x,p$ with $a,a^\dagger$; then $\langle a\rangle=\alpha(t)$ and $\langle a^\dagger\rangle=\bar\alpha(t)$, so $\langle x\rangle\propto\mathrm{Re}\,\alpha(t)$, $\langle p\rangle\propto\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha(t)$: a point going round a circle, which is exactly the classical oscillator. Ehrenfest (sheet 2) is exact here because the force is linear.

steps.reveal: With $aa^\dagger=a^\dagger a+1$: $\langle x^2\rangle=\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}(1+2|\alpha|^2+\alpha^2+\bar\alpha^2)$, so $(\Delta x)^2=\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}$, $(\Delta p)^2=\frac{m\hbar\omega}2$, $\Delta x\Delta p=\hbar/2$ at all times.
steps.explain: For $\langle x^2\rangle$ expand $(a+a^\dagger)^2$ and bring every $a$ to the right ($aa^\dagger=a^\dagger a+1$); then $a$ acts on the right ket and $a^\dagger$ on the left bra as $\alpha$, $\bar\alpha$. The only $\alpha$-independent leftover is the 1: $(\Delta x)^2=\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}$, the ground-state value. Coherent states are shifted ground states: minimal uncertainty forever.

steps.reveal: Polar coordinates $\alpha=re^{i\theta}$, $d\alpha^*d\alpha=2i\,r\,dr\,d\theta$: the $\theta$ integral gives $2\pi\delta_{nm}$, then $\frac{2}{n!}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r^{2n+1}dr=\frac{\Gamma(n+1)}{n!}=1$: $\sum_n|n\rangle\langle n|=I$.
steps.explain: Polar coordinates in the complex plane: the angular integral of $e^{i(n-m)\theta}$ is $2\pi\delta_{nm}$, so only diagonal terms $|n\rangle\langle n|$ survive; the radial integral is a Gamma function equal to $n!$, which cancels the $1/n!$. What is left is $\sum_n|n\rangle\langle n|=I$. (Coherent states are overcomplete: not orthogonal, but they still resolve the identity.)

steps.reveal: $\left(\sqrt{\frac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}x+\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}}\frac{d}{dx}\right)\psi_\alpha=\alpha\psi_\alpha$ gives $\psi_\alpha=A\exp\left[-\frac{m\omega}{2\hbar}\left(x-\sqrt{\frac{2\hbar}{m\omega}}\alpha\right)^2\right]$. For $\alpha=0$ it is the ground state, which we already knew is Gaussian.
steps.explain: In position space $a$ is the differential operator $\sqrt{\frac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}x+\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}}\frac{d}{dx}$. The eigenvalue equation is first order, $\psi'=(\text{linear in }x)\psi$, so $\psi$ is the exponential of a quadratic: the ground-state Gaussian shifted to the centre $\sqrt{2\hbar/m\omega}\,\alpha$.

enc.title: Sheet 7 Q4: Degeneracies

source.where: Exercise sheet VII, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 7.pdf

enc.goal: $D_n^k$ = number of ways to write $n$ as a sum of $k$ non-negative integers; $F^k(s)=\sum_nD_n^ks^n$, $|s|<1$. (i) Show $F^k(s)=\sum_{n_1}\cdots\sum_{n_k}s^{n_1+\dots+n_k}$. (ii) Deduce $F^k=(1-s)^{-k}$ and $D_n^k=\binom{n+k-1}{n}$. (iii) Degeneracies of the isotropic oscillator in 2D and 3D.

steps.reveal: $\prod_j\left(\sum_{n_j}s^{n_j}\right)=\sum_nc_ns^n$ where $c_n$ counts the terms with $n_1+\dots+n_k=n$, i.e. $c_n=D_n^k$.
steps.explain: Multiplying out a product of $k$ series gives every term $s^{n_1}\cdots s^{n_k}=s^{n_1+\dots+n_k}$ once. Collecting all terms with the same total $n$, their number is by definition $D_n^k$. This is a generating function: counting turned into algebra.

steps.reveal: Each factor is $(1-s)^{-1}$, so $F^k=(1-s)^{-k}=\sum_n\binom{n+k-1}{n}s^n$ (binomial series or $\frac{1}{(k-1)!}\frac{d^{k-1}}{ds^{k-1}}\frac1{1-s}$).
steps.explain: Each factor is a geometric series $\frac1{1-s}$, so $F^k=(1-s)^{-k}$. Its Taylor coefficients follow from the binomial series (or from differentiating $\frac1{1-s}$ $k-1$ times): $\binom{n+k-1}{n}$, the "stars and bars" count.

A $k$-dimensional isotropic oscillator has energy $\hbar\omega(n_1+\dots+n_k+\frac k2)$: the degeneracy of level $N$ is the number of ways to distribute $N$ quanta over $k$ directions, $D_N^k$. For $k=2$: $N+1$; for $k=3$: $\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}{2}$.

sheets.title: Angular momentum, so(4), su(2) in the 2D oscillator

enc.title: Sheet 8 Q1: Angular momentum

source.where: Exercise sheet VIII, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 8.pdf

enc.goal: $\vec L=\vec r\wedge\vec p$, $L_i=\varepsilon_{ijk}r_jp_k$. (i) With $[r_i,p_j]=i\hbar\delta_{ij}$ derive $[L_i,L_j]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k$ and $[L_3,\vec L^2]=0$. (ii) Evaluate $[L_3,L_1L_2+L_2L_1]$ and deduce $\langle l,m|L_1^2|l,m\rangle=\langle l,m|L_2^2|l,m\rangle=\frac{\hbar^2}2[l(l+1)-m^2]$. Hint: for an eigenstate $|\psi\rangle$ of a self-adjoint $A$, $\langle\psi|[A,B]|\psi\rangle=0$.

steps.reveal: $[L_i,L_j]=\varepsilon_{ikl}\varepsilon_{jmn}[r_kp_l,r_mp_n]=i\hbar(-\varepsilon_{ikl}\varepsilon_{jln}r_kp_n+\varepsilon_{ikl}\varepsilon_{jmk}r_mp_l)$; with $\varepsilon\varepsilon=\delta\delta-\delta\delta$ this is $i\hbar(r_ip_j-r_jp_i)=i\hbar\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k$, since $\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k=r_ip_j-r_jp_i$.
steps.explain: Strategy: write both $L$'s with $\varepsilon$ and use $[AB,CD]$-rules: the only non-zero basic commutator is $[r_k,p_n]=i\hbar\delta_{kn}$, so $[r_kp_l,r_mp_n]=r_k[p_l,r_m]p_n+r_m[r_k,p_n]p_l$, each term giving one Kronecker delta. Then contract two $\varepsilon$'s with $\varepsilon_{ikl}\varepsilon_{imn}=\delta_{km}\delta_{ln}-\delta_{kn}\delta_{lm}$ and recognise $r_ip_j-r_jp_i=\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k$.

Product rule for commutators: $[A,BC]=[A,B]C+B[A,C]$. Apply it to $L_1^2$ and $L_2^2$ and insert $[L_3,L_1]=i\hbar L_2$, $[L_3,L_2]=-i\hbar L_1$: the four terms cancel in pairs. ($[L_3,L_3^2]=0$ trivially.) So $\vec L^2$ and $L_3$ can be diagonalised together.

steps.reveal: $A|\psi\rangle=a|\psi\rangle$ with $a$ real: $\langle\psi|AB-BA|\psi\rangle=(a-a)\langle\psi|B|\psi\rangle=0$.
steps.explain: The hint in one line: $\langle\psi|AB|\psi\rangle=a\langle\psi|B|\psi\rangle$ (A acts to the left on the bra, allowed because $A$ is self-adjoint and $a$ real) and $\langle\psi|BA|\psi\rangle=a\langle\psi|B|\psi\rangle$ (A acts to the right). The difference vanishes.

steps.reveal: $[L_3,L_1L_2+L_2L_1]=2i\hbar(L_2^2-L_1^2)$, so in $|l,m\rangle$: $\langle L_1^2\rangle=\langle L_2^2\rangle$. With $L_1^2+L_2^2=\vec L^2-L_3^2$: each is $\frac{\hbar^2}2[l(l+1)-m^2]$ (and $\langle L_{1,2}\rangle=0$, so these are the variances).
steps.explain: Use the hint with $A=L_3$: the commutator $[L_3,L_1L_2+L_2L_1]$ works out to $2i\hbar(L_2^2-L_1^2)$, and its expectation in an $L_3$ eigenstate is zero. So $\langle L_1^2\rangle=\langle L_2^2\rangle$. Their sum is $\langle\vec L^2-L_3^2\rangle=\hbar^2[l(l+1)-m^2]$; each gets half. Even with $m=l$ this is not zero: the angular momentum can never point exactly along $z$.

enc.title: Sheet 8 Q2: SO(4)

source.where: Exercise sheet VIII, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 8.pdf

enc.goal: so(4) = tangent vectors at the identity of paths in SO(4). (i) Describe so(4) as a space of matrices. (ii) Find a basis $A_i,B_i$ with $[A_i,A_j]=\varepsilon_{ijk}A_k$, $[B_i,B_j]=\varepsilon_{ijk}A_k$, $[A_i,B_j]=\varepsilon_{ijk}B_k$. (iii) Show so(4) $\cong$ su(2) $\oplus$ su(2).

steps.reveal: $\gamma^T\gamma=I$ gives $\dot\gamma(0)^T+\dot\gamma(0)=0$; conversely $e^{tM}$ for antisymmetric $M$ is in SO(4). So so(4) = real antisymmetric $4\times4$ matrices, 6-dimensional.
steps.explain: Lie algebra = velocities at the identity. Differentiate $\gamma(t)^T\gamma(t)=I$ at $t=0$ (where $\gamma=I$): $\dot\gamma^T+\dot\gamma=0$, so the tangent vectors are antisymmetric. Conversely every antisymmetric $M$ gives the path $e^{tM}$ in SO(4). A $4\times4$ antisymmetric matrix has $\binom42=6$ free entries: one rotation per plane of coordinates.

steps.reveal: $A_i$: rotations in the 3D block $(1,2,3)$, $(A_i)_{jk}=-\varepsilon_{ijk}$ ($A_1$ rotates in the 2-3 plane, etc.); $B_i$: the "boosts" mixing coordinate $i$ with the 4th, $(B_i)_{4i}=1$, $(B_i)_{i4}=-1$. Compute $[A_1,A_2]=A_3$, $[B_1,B_2]=A_3$, $[A_1,B_2]=B_3$, $[A_1,B_3]=-B_2$, $[A_1,B_1]=0$; the rest follows by cyclic permutation of $1,2,3$.
steps.explain: Split the 6 planes: three planes inside the first three coordinates (ordinary rotations $A_i$, which satisfy the so(3) relations) and three planes mixing coordinate $i$ with the fourth ($B_i$). Compute the matrix commutators explicitly for a few pairs; the others follow by relabelling 1→2→3.

steps.reveal: $X_i=\frac12(A_i+B_i)$, $Y_i=\frac12(A_i-B_i)$: $[X_i,X_j]=\varepsilon_{ijk}X_k$, $[Y_i,Y_j]=\varepsilon_{ijk}Y_k$, $[X_i,Y_j]=0$. In hydrogen these are $\frac12(\vec L\pm\vec D)$ built from $\vec L$ and the Runge-Lenz vector: the origin of the $n^2$ degeneracy.
steps.explain: Decouple: the combinations $X=\frac12(A+B)$ and $Y=\frac12(A-B)$ each close on themselves and commute with each other: two independent copies of su(2). In hydrogen $\vec L$ and the Runge–Lenz vector play the roles of $A$ and $B$, so the symmetry is two commuting "spins", and that is what produces the $n^2$ degeneracy (sheet 11).

keyPoints: link to $\vec L$ and Runge-Lenz in hydrogen

questions.title: Representations of su(2) and the 2D oscillator

enc.title: Sheet 8 Q3: Representations of su(2) and the 2D oscillator

source.where: Exercise sheet VIII, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 8.pdf

enc.goal: $J_3=\frac12(a^\dagger a-b^\dagger b)$, $J_+=a^\dagger b$, $J_-=b^\dagger a$. (i) Show $[J_3,J_\pm]=\pm J_\pm$, $[J_+,J_-]=2J_3$. (ii) Show $\vec J^2=\frac N2(\frac N2+1)$, $N=N_a+N_b$. (iii) Give $J_\pm,J_3$ on $|n_a,n_b\rangle$. (iv) With $j=\frac{n_a+n_b}2$, $m=\frac{n_a-n_b}2$ get the standard su(2) form and $|j,m\rangle=\frac{(a^\dagger)^{j+m}(b^\dagger)^{j-m}}{\sqrt{(j+m)!(j-m)!}}|0,0\rangle$. (v) Show the $J$’s commute with $a^\dagger a+b^\dagger b$.

steps.reveal: Using $[a,a^\dagger]=1$ and that $a$’s commute with $b$’s: $2[J_3,J_+]=a^\dagger b+a^\dagger b$, $2[J_3,J_-]=-2b^\dagger a$, $[J_+,J_-]=a^\dagger(1+b^\dagger b)a-b^\dagger(1+a^\dagger a)b=a^\dagger a-b^\dagger b=2J_3$.
steps.explain: Tools: $[a,a^\dagger]=1$, $[b,b^\dagger]=1$, everything with $a$ commutes with everything with $b$. Each $J$ is quadratic, so each commutator reduces to one use of $[a,a^\dagger]=1$ or $[b,b^\dagger]=1$. For $[J_+,J_-]$: $a^\dagger bb^\dagger a-b^\dagger aa^\dagger b$; use $bb^\dagger=1+b^\dagger b$ and $aa^\dagger=1+a^\dagger a$; the quartic terms cancel, leaving $a^\dagger a-b^\dagger b=2J_3$.

steps.reveal: $\vec J^2=\frac14(N_a-N_b)^2+\frac12\left(N_a(1+N_b)+N_b(1+N_a)\right)=\frac14(N_a+N_b)^2+\frac12(N_a+N_b)=\frac N2\left(\frac N2+1\right)$.
steps.explain: $\vec J^2=J_3^2+\frac12(J_+J_-+J_-J_+)$. Express everything with number operators $N_a=a^\dagger a$, $N_b=b^\dagger b$ (again using $aa^\dagger=N_a+1$); it simplifies to $\frac N2(\frac N2+1)$, i.e. $j(j+1)$ with $j=N/2$.

steps.reveal: $J_+|n_a,n_b\rangle=\sqrt{n_b(n_a+1)}|n_a+1,n_b-1\rangle$, $J_-|n_a,n_b\rangle=\sqrt{n_a(n_b+1)}|n_a-1,n_b+1\rangle$, $J_3=\frac12(n_a-n_b)$. With $n_a=j+m$, $n_b=j-m$: $J_\pm|j,m\rangle=\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m\pm1)}|j,m\pm1\rangle$, $J_3|j,m\rangle=m|j,m\rangle$: the spin-$j$ representation (Schwinger representation).
steps.explain: Action on number states: $J_+=a^\dagger b$ moves one quantum from $b$ to $a$ with the usual square-root factors. Relabel $n_a=j+m$, $n_b=j-m$: the factor $\sqrt{n_b(n_a+1)}=\sqrt{(j-m)(j+m+1)}=\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m+1)}$, the standard spin formula. Two oscillators "are" a spin: Schwinger's trick.

steps.reveal: $[J_+,N_a+N_b]=[a^\dagger,N_a]b+a^\dagger[b,N_b]=-a^\dagger b+a^\dagger b=0$, same for $J_-$, $J_3$. The level $E=\hbar\omega(N+1)$ is the spin $j=N/2$ multiplet: dimension $N+1$, exactly its degeneracy.
steps.explain: $J_+$ moves a quantum but does not create or destroy one, so $N=N_a+N_b$ is unchanged: the $J$'s commute with $N$, hence with $H$. Each energy level $N$ is the spin-$N/2$ multiplet, dimension $N+1$, which explains the degeneracy found in sheet 7.

sheets.title: sech² potential, discrete spectra, Pauli matrices, su(3)

enc.title: Sheet 9 Q1: The sech² potential

source.where: Exercise sheet IX, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 9.pdf

enc.goal: $H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2+V$, $V=-\frac{\hbar^2}{m}\mathrm{sech}^2x$. (i) Sketch $V$ and the expected ground state. (ii) Show $A^\dagger A\psi=(\epsilon+1)\psi$ with $\epsilon=2mE/\hbar^2$, $A=\partial_x+\tanh x$. (iii) Show $\epsilon\ge-1$ and find $\psi_0$ (what is $A\psi_0$?).

steps.reveal: Symmetric well with minimum $-\hbar^2/m$ at $x=0$, going to 0 at $\pm\infty$. Ground state: even, no node, localised in the well, decaying outside.
steps.explain: $\mathrm{sech}^2x=1/\cosh^2x$ is a bell: 1 at $x=0$, decaying like $4e^{-2|x|}$. So $V$ is a smooth well of depth $\hbar^2/m$. A ground state is even, without nodes, and decays outside.

steps.reveal: $A^\dagger=-\partial_x+\tanh x$, $A^\dagger A\psi=-\psi^{\prime\prime}+(\tanh^2x-\tanh^\prime x)\psi=-\psi^{\prime\prime}+(1-2\,\mathrm{sech}^2x)\psi=\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}H\psi+\psi=(\epsilon+1)\psi$.
steps.explain: Factorisation method: write $H$ (up to a constant) as $A^\dagger A$. Compute $(-\partial_x+\tanh)(\partial_x+\tanh)\psi=-\psi''-\tanh'\psi+\tanh^2\psi$ (the cross terms $\pm\tanh\,\psi'$ cancel). With $\tanh'=\mathrm{sech}^2$ and $\tanh^2=1-\mathrm{sech}^2$: $-\psi''+(1-2\mathrm{sech}^2x)\psi$, which is $\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}H\psi+\psi$.

steps.reveal: $\langle\chi|A^\dagger A|\chi\rangle=\|A\chi\|^2\ge0$ gives $\epsilon\ge-1$, saturated when $A\psi_0=0$: $\psi_0^\prime=-\tanh x\,\psi_0$, $\psi_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt2\cosh x}$, $E_0=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}$.
steps.explain: Why $A^\dagger A\ge0$: $\langle\chi|A^\dagger A|\chi\rangle=\langle A\chi|A\chi\rangle=\|A\chi\|^2$. So $\epsilon+1\ge0$ for every eigenvalue, with equality exactly when $A\psi=0$, a first-order equation: $\psi'=-\tanh x\,\psi$, solved by $1/\cosh x$. This is the same trick as $a|0\rangle=0$ for the oscillator.

keyPoints: shape of $V$ and an even, nodeless $\psi_0$
enc.primer:
The question in plain words

For most potentials the Schrödinger equation is a second-order differential equation you cannot solve by hand. But for a few special potentials there is a shortcut that gives you the ground state from a first-order equation, which you can always integrate. It is the same trick that makes the "elegant solution" of the harmonic oscillator work. This question shows that the trick is not special to the oscillator.

The picture

Think of factorising a number: if you can write $H$ (up to a constant) as $A^\dagger A$, then $H$ can never go below that constant, because $A^\dagger A$ is "a square": $\langle\psi|A^\dagger A|\psi\rangle=\|A\psi\|^2\ge0$. The lowest state is the one that $A$ squashes to zero. So instead of solving $H\psi=E\psi$ you solve $A\psi_0=0$.

The pieces you need

  • Oscillator (script 6.14–6.18): $a=\frac1{\sqrt2}(x+\partial_x)$, $H=\hbar\omega(a^\dagger a+\frac12)$. Meaning: the energy is $\frac12\hbar\omega$ plus a non-negative part.
  • Positivity (6.25): $\langle n|a^\dagger a|n\rangle=\|a|n\rangle\|^2=n\ge0$. Meaning: the spectrum is bounded from below.
  • Ground state (6.28): $a|0\rangle=0$, in position space $(x+\partial_x)\psi_0=0$, a first-order equation: $\psi_0\propto e^{-x^2/2}$.
  • General version: with $A=\partial_x+W(x)$ one finds $A^\dagger A=-\partial_x^2+W^2-W^\prime$. If your potential (in suitable units) is $W^2-W^\prime$ plus a constant, you win.

Tiny example

Take $W=x$: $A=\partial_x+x=\sqrt2\,a$ and $A^\dagger A=-\partial_x^2+x^2-1$. That is $\frac{2}{\hbar\omega}H-1$ for the oscillator, so $E_0=\frac12\hbar\omega$, and $A\psi_0=0$ gives $\psi_0^\prime=-x\psi_0$, the Gaussian. Two lines instead of a power series.

What this sheet question needs

The sheet gives you $W=\tanh x$. Check $W^2-W^\prime=\tanh^2x-\mathrm{sech}^2x=1-2\,\mathrm{sech}^2x$: exactly $\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}V+1$. So $A^\dagger A\psi=(\epsilon+1)\psi$, positivity gives $\epsilon\ge-1$, and $A\psi_0=0$ means $\psi_0^\prime=-\tanh x\,\psi_0$, i.e. $\psi_0\propto1/\cosh x$. For the sketch (part i): an even, node-free bump sitting in the well.

Read in the script

§6.1.2 "Die elegante Lösung", pp. 61–63, eqs. (6.14)–(6.18), the positivity argument around (6.25)–(6.28), and the ground state (6.31). The factorisation for other potentials is not in the script: it is the point of this exercise.

enc.title: Sheet 9 Q2: Partner potentials

source.where: Exercise sheet IX (HS26), Question 2 (new this year); official solution: sheet_9_solutions.pdf

enc.goal: (i) $H_\pm=-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+q^2(x)\pm q^\prime(x)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R)$, $q$ real. Show: (a) $\langle\psi|H_\pm|\psi\rangle\ge0$; (b) $H_+$ and $H_-$ have the same eigenvalues $\lambda$, except possibly $\lambda=0$; (c) $\lambda=0$ is an eigenvalue of at most one partner: for which $q$, and which partner? (The answer is topological: it does not change if $q$ is modified on a bounded interval.) (ii) Describe the partner potentials for $q=x+gx^2$ ($g$ small), show $H_\pm$ are unitarily equivalent for $g\ne0$, discuss $g\to0$ in view of (c). Hint: reflection about $x_0=-1/2g$.

steps.reveal: $q=x$ gives the oscillator $H_\pm=-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+x^2\pm1$. In general set $a=q+\frac d{dx}$, $a^\dagger=q-\frac d{dx}$: $[a,a^\dagger]=2q^\prime$, and $a^\dagger a=-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+q^2-q^\prime=H_-$, $aa^\dagger=H_+$.
$\langle\psi|H_-|\psi\rangle=\|a\psi\|^2\ge0$, $\langle\psi|H_+|\psi\rangle=\|a^\dagger\psi\|^2\ge0$.

If $H_-\psi=\lambda\psi$ then $H_+(a\psi)=aa^\dagger a\psi=\lambda\,a\psi$ with $\|a\psi\|^2=\lambda\|\psi\|^2$: for $\lambda\ne0$, $a\psi\ne0$ is an eigenvector of $H_+$. Likewise $a^\dagger$ maps eigenvectors of $H_+$ to $H_-$. So the nonzero eigenvalues agree, with equal multiplicities.

$H_-\psi=0\iff a\psi=0$: $\psi^\prime+q\psi=0$, $\psi_-=e^{-Q}$ with $Q^\prime=q$. $H_+\psi=0\iff a^\dagger\psi=0$: $\psi_+=e^{+Q}$. Both normalisable is impossible: $\langle\psi_-|\psi_+\rangle=\int e^{-Q}e^{Q}dx=\infty$. So $\lambda=0$ belongs to $H_-$ iff $e^{-Q}\in L^2$ ($Q\to+\infty$ at both ends, e.g. $q>0$ far right, $q<0$ far left: the oscillator), to $H_+$ iff $e^{+Q}\in L^2$. Changing $q$ on a bounded interval only changes $Q$ by constants outside it: the answer depends only on the asymptotics.

$q^2\pm q^\prime=x^2(1+gx)^2\pm(1+2gx)$: double wells with minima near $x=0$ and $x=-1/g$; the sign $\pm$ decides which is deeper. The reflection $(U\psi)(x)=\psi(-x-1/g)$ about $x_0=-\frac1{2g}$ maps $x^2(1+gx)^2$ to itself and $1+2gx\to-(1+2gx)$: $U^*H_+U=H_-$. So $\lambda=0$ is an eigenvalue of both or neither; by (c) neither: $Q=\frac{x^2}2+\frac{gx^3}3\to\pm\infty$ for $x\to\pm\infty$, so $e^{\pm Q}$ is never normalisable. For $g\to0$ one well escapes to $-\infty$; at $g=0$ the oscillator remains, $Q\to+\infty$ at both ends and $H_-$ has the zero mode $e^{-x^2/2}$.

$q=x+gx^2$: reflection about $-1/2g$ swaps $H_\pm$, no zero mode

enc.title: Sheet 9 Q3: Stability of the hydrogen atom

source.where: Exercise sheet IX (HS26), Question 3 (new this year); official solution: sheet_9_solutions.pdf

enc.goal: $H=\frac{\vec p^2}{2m}-\frac{e^2}{|\vec x|}$ is bounded below quantum mechanically. (i) From $\langle p_i^2\rangle\ge(\Delta p_i)^2$ (likewise for $x_i$) one gets $\langle\vec p^2\rangle\langle\vec x^2\rangle\ge\sum_i\langle p_i^2\rangle\langle x_i^2\rangle\ge\frac{3\hbar^2}4$ and hence $\langle H\rangle\ge\frac{3\hbar^2}{8m}\frac1{\langle\vec x^2\rangle}-e^2\left\langle\frac1{|\vec x|}\right\rangle$. Show that this does not prove stability: some states make the right side arbitrarily negative. Hint: superpose one wave function outside the Bohr radius $a_0=\hbar^2/me^2$ and one inside $\varepsilon a_0$. (ii) Use the Hardy inequality $\left\langle\frac{\vec p^2}{\hbar^2}\right\rangle\ge\left\langle\frac1{4\vec x^2}\right\rangle$ to show $H\ge-C$, $C>0$.

steps.reveal: $\psi=\frac1{\sqrt2}(\psi_++\psi_-)$, normalised pieces with $\mathrm{supp}\,\psi_+\subset\{|\vec x|>a_0\}$, $\mathrm{supp}\,\psi_-\subset\{|\vec x|<\varepsilon a_0\}$. Disjoint supports: $\langle f\rangle_\psi=\frac12(\langle f\rangle_++\langle f\rangle_-)$ for every $f(\vec x)$. So $\langle\vec x^2\rangle\ge\frac{a_0^2}2$ (from the far piece) and $\left\langle\frac1{|\vec x|}\right\rangle\ge\frac1{2\varepsilon a_0}$ (from the near piece).

The lower bound is at most $\frac{3\hbar^2}{8m}\frac2{a_0^2}-\frac{e^2}{2\varepsilon a_0}=\frac{e^2}{a_0}\left(\frac34-\frac1{2\varepsilon}\right)\to-\infty$ for $\varepsilon\to0$ (using $\frac{\hbar^2}{ma_0^2}=\frac{e^2}{a_0}$). The heuristic fails because $\langle\vec x^2\rangle$ can be kept large by a far piece while a near piece makes $\langle1/r\rangle$ huge.

$H=\frac{e^2}{a_0}\left(\frac{a_0^2}2\frac{\vec p^2}{\hbar^2}-\frac{a_0}{|\vec x|}\right)$, so with Hardy $\langle H\rangle\ge\frac{e^2}{8a_0}\left\langle s^2-8s\right\rangle$ with $s=\frac{a_0}{|\vec x|}$. Since $s^2-8s=(s-4)^2-16\ge-16$: $\langle H\rangle\ge-\frac{2e^2}{a_0}$, so $C=\frac{2e^2}{a_0}$ (four times the true binding $\frac{e^2}{2a_0}=13.6$ eV). Hardy works because it bounds $\langle1/r^2\rangle$ by the kinetic energy locally, not through $\langle r^2\rangle$.

enc.title: Sheet 9 Q4: Discreteness of the spectrum

Take the trace in position states: $e^{-\beta V}$ is just a number there; for $e^{-\beta T}$ insert momentum states ($T$ is diagonal there) with $|\langle q|p\rangle|^2=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d}$. The result is the classical partition function: quantum $Z$ is bounded by classical $Z$.

Sufficient: $\int d^dq\,e^{- eta V(q)}<\infty$ for all $ eta>0$. For $
u\|q\|^\alpha$: $\mathrm{vol}(S^{d-1})\int_0^\infty r^{d-1}e^{- eta
