enc.primer:
The question in plain words

Measuring the energy can give either isolated values (an electron bound in an atom) or a whole continuum (a free electron). The question: can you tell which, without solving the Schrödinger equation, just by looking at the potential? Yes: if the particle is confined everywhere, the spectrum is discrete. This question makes that intuition precise.

The picture

Semiclassically, every quantum state occupies a cell of size $2\pi\hbar$ in phase space $(q,p)$ (per dimension). If the classically allowed region below any energy $E$ has finite phase-space area, it contains only finitely many cells: finitely many states below $E$, a discrete spectrum. A free particle can sit anywhere: infinite area, infinitely many states at every energy: a continuum. The "thermometer" that counts the states is the partition function $Z(\beta)=\mathrm{tr}\,e^{-\beta H}$.

The pieces you need

  • Spectrum (4.37–4.41): the possible measurement results. Free particle $\sigma(H)=\mathbb R_+$ (continuous), finite well $\{E_1,\dots,E_N\}\cup\mathbb R_+$ (mixed), oscillator $\{\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)\}$ (discrete).
  • Spectral theorem (4.42): $f(H)=\sum_Ef(E)P_E$. With $f=e^{-\beta E}$: $Z(\beta)=\sum_n e^{-\beta E_n}$ (with degeneracy). A finite answer needs countably many, well-separated levels.
  • Golden-Thompson: $\mathrm{tr}\,e^{A+B}\le\mathrm{tr}(e^Ae^B)$. It lets you split kinetic and potential energy as if they commuted, with an inequality instead of an equality.
  • Outcome: $Z_{\rm quantum}\le Z_{\rm classical}=\frac1{(2\pi\hbar)^d}\int d^dq\,d^dp\,e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$.

Tiny example

Oscillator: $Z_{\rm q}=\sum_ne^{-\beta\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)}=\frac{1}{2\sinh(\beta\hbar\omega/2)}$, $Z_{\rm cl}=\frac{1}{2\pi\hbar}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\beta m\omega^2}}=\frac1{\beta\hbar\omega}$. Both finite, and indeed $\frac1{2\sinh(x/2)}\le\frac1x$. Free particle: the $q$ integral is $\int dq=\infty$: no discreteness.

What this sheet question needs

(i) Argue "finite trace means discrete" (a continuum makes the trace infinite, e.g. $\langle p|p\rangle=\delta(0)$). (ii) Apply Golden-Thompson to $e^{-\beta(T+V)}$, take the trace in position states, insert momentum states for $e^{-\beta T}$: you get exactly the classical integral. (iii) The $p$-integral is always a Gaussian, so the criterion is $\int d^dq\,e^{-\beta V(q)}<\infty$; for $V=\nu\|q\|^\alpha$ substitute $t=\beta\nu r^\alpha$ to get a Gamma function.

Read in the script

§4.6 "Verallgemeinerung auf ∞-dimensionale Hilberträume", pp. 48–49: definition of the spectrum (4.37), the three examples (4.39–4.41) and the spectral theorem (4.42–4.47). The partition function and Golden-Thompson are not in the script; they are introduced by this exercise.

enc.title: Sheet 9 Q5: Unitary transformations

source.where: Exercise sheet IX (HS26), Question 5 (new this year); official solution: sheet_9_solutions.pdf

enc.goal: $\hbar=1$. $U_m(v,t)=\exp\left(-iv(\hat Pt-m\hat X)\right)$, $m,v,t$ real. (i) Show $U_m$ is unitary. (ii) Compute $e^{-iv\hat Pt}e^{ivm\hat X}$ and show $U_m\ne e^{-iv\hat Pt}e^{ivm\hat X}$ in general. (iii) Show $U_m|x\rangle\propto|x+vt\rangle$, $U_m|p\rangle\propto|p+mv\rangle$. (iv) Compute $U_m\hat XU_m^\dagger$ and $U_m\hat PU_m^\dagger$.

steps.reveal: $v(\hat Pt-m\hat X)$ is hermitian ($v,t,m$ real, $\hat X,\hat P$ hermitian), so its exponential with $-i$ is unitary.

$e^Ae^B=e^{A+B+\frac12[A,B]}$ when $[A,B]$ is a number. Here $[-iv\hat Pt,ivm\hat X]=v^2tm[\hat P,\hat X]=-iv^2tm$, so $e^{-iv\hat Pt}e^{ivm\hat X}=e^{-iv\hat Pt+ivm\hat X-\frac{i}2v^2tm}=U_m\,e^{-\frac i2v^2tm}$: they differ by a phase (equal only if $v^2tm=0$ mod $4\pi$).

$U_m=e^{\frac i2v^2tm}e^{-iv\hat Pt}e^{ivm\hat X}$, and $e^{-iv\hat Pt}|x\rangle=|x+vt\rangle$ (a translation: $\langle p|e^{-ivt\hat P}|x\rangle=e^{-ipvt}\langle p|x\rangle=\langle p|x+vt\rangle$). So $U_m|x\rangle=e^{\frac i2v^2tm}e^{ivmx}|x+vt\rangle$. Ordered the other way, $U_m=e^{-\frac i2v^2tm}e^{ivm\hat X}e^{-iv\hat Pt}$ and $e^{ivm\hat X}$ shifts momentum: $U_m|p\rangle=e^{-\frac i2v^2tm}e^{-ivpt}|p+mv\rangle$.

$U_m\hat XU_m^\dagger=\int x\,|x+vt\rangle\langle x+vt|\,dx=\hat X-vt$, and likewise $U_m\hat PU_m^\dagger=\hat P-mv$. $U_m$ is the Galilean boost by $v$ at time $t$ (compare sheet 1 Q3): positions shift by $vt$, momenta by $mv$.

keyPoints: BCH with $[\hat X,\hat P]=i$: only a phase $e^{\mp\frac i2v^2tm}$
$U\hat XU^\dagger=\hat X-vt$, $U\hat PU^\dagger=\hat P-mv$: Galilean boost

enc.title: Sheet 9 Q6: The Aharonov–Bohm effect

source.where: Exercise sheet IX (HS26), Question 6 (new this year); official solution: sheet_9_solutions.pdf

enc.goal: Electron (charge $-e$), $i\hbar\partial_t\psi=\left[\frac1{2m}\left(-i\hbar\nabla+\frac ec\vec A\right)^2-e\phi\right]\psi$, $\phi=0$. (i) In a simply connected region $G$ where $\vec B=0$ (outside a long coil), compare $\psi_0$ (field off everywhere) and $\psi_B$ (field on) with the same initial and boundary data after gauging $\vec A$ to zero in $G$ (gauge function zero at $\vec x_0$). Show $\psi_B(\vec x)=\psi_0(\vec x)\exp\left(-\frac{ie}{\hbar c}\int_{\vec x_0}^{\vec x}d\vec s\cdot\vec A\right)$. (ii) A double slit with the coil inside the middle wall: the electrons never meet $\vec B$. With $\psi_\sigma=\psi_{1,\sigma}+\psi_{2,\sigma}$ ($\sigma=0$ field off, $B$ on), compute $I_B=|\psi_B|^2$ in terms of $\psi_{1,0}$, $\psi_{2,0}$ and the flux $\Phi_B$.

steps.reveal: $\nabla\times\vec A=0$ in simply connected $G$: $\vec A=\nabla\Lambda$ with $\Lambda(\vec x)=\int_{\vec x_0}^{\vec x}d\vec s\cdot\vec A$ (path independent in $G$). The gauge $\chi=-\Lambda$ gives $\vec A^\prime=0$ and $\tilde\psi_B=e^{ie\Lambda/\hbar c}\psi_B$, which solves the field-free equation with the same data, so $\tilde\psi_B=\psi_0$ and $\psi_B=\psi_0\,e^{-\frac{ie}{\hbar c}\Lambda}$.

Apply (i) in a simply connected neighbourhood of each slit path, same reference point at the source: $\psi_{j,B}=\psi_{j,0}\exp\left(-\frac{ie}{\hbar c}\int_jd\vec s\cdot\vec A\right)$, $j=1,2$. The two path integrals differ by a closed loop around the coil: $\int_1-\int_2=\oint d\vec s\cdot\vec A=\Phi_B$ (Stokes). So $\psi_B=\left[\psi_{1,0}e^{-\frac{ie}{\hbar c}\Phi_B}+\psi_{2,0}\right]e^{-\frac{ie}{\hbar c}\int_2d\vec s\cdot\vec A}$.

$I_B=|\psi_{1,0}|^2+|\psi_{2,0}|^2+2\,\mathrm{Re}\left\{\psi_{1,0}\psi_{2,0}^*\,e^{-\frac{ie}{\hbar c}\Phi_B}\right\}$: the fringes shift with the enclosed flux although $\vec B=0$ along both paths, periodic in $\Phi_B$ with period $\frac{2\pi\hbar c}e=\frac{hc}e$ (the flux quantum). The vector potential, through a gauge-invariant loop integral, is physical in quantum mechanics.

keyPoints: $\vec B=0$ in simply connected $G$: $\vec A=\nabla\Lambda$, gauge it away
phase difference $\frac e{\hbar c}\oint\vec A\cdot d\vec s=\frac{e\Phi_B}{\hbar c}$

enc.title: Sheet 9 Q7: Pauli matrices and rotations

source.where: Exercise sheet IX, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 9.pdf

enc.goal: Show that $U(\omega\vec n)=\exp(-i\frac\omega2\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma)\in SU(2)$ is a rotation by $\omega$ about $\vec n$: (i) $\sigma_j\sigma_k=\delta_{jk}I+i\varepsilon_{jkl}\sigma_l$; (ii) $U=\cos\frac\omega2I-i\sin\frac\omega2\,\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma$; (iii) with $\tilde x=\vec x\cdot\vec\sigma$, compute $\tilde x^\prime=U\tilde xU^\dagger$.

steps.reveal: Check $\sigma_j^2=I$ and $\sigma_1\sigma_2=i\sigma_3$ (cyclic); hence $(\vec x\cdot\vec\sigma)(\vec y\cdot\vec\sigma)=(\vec x\cdot\vec y)I+i(\vec x\times\vec y)\cdot\vec\sigma$ and $(\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma)^2=I$.
steps.explain: Check the products on the explicit matrices: $\sigma_j^2=I$, $\sigma_1\sigma_2=i\sigma_3$ and cyclic, and different $\sigma$'s anticommute. The combined formula $(\vec x\cdot\vec\sigma)(\vec y\cdot\vec\sigma)=\vec x\cdot\vec y+i(\vec x\times\vec y)\cdot\vec\sigma$ follows by summing over components; for $\vec x=\vec y=\vec n$ (unit vector) the cross product vanishes: $(\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma)^2=I$.

steps.reveal: Split the series into even powers ($I$) and odd powers ($\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma$): $\cos\frac\omega2I-i\sin\frac\omega2\,\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma$. Note $U(2\pi\vec n)=-I$: spinors change sign under a full turn.
steps.explain: Because $(\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma)^2=I$, even powers in the exponential series are $I$ and odd powers are $\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma$. The even part sums to $\cos\frac\omega2$, the odd part to $\sin\frac\omega2$, exactly like $e^{i\phi}=\cos\phi+i\sin\phi$. The half angle means a $2\pi$ rotation gives $-I$.

steps.reveal: $\tilde x^\prime=\left(\cos\omega\,\vec x-\sin\omega\,\vec x\times\vec n+(1-\cos\omega)(\vec x\cdot\vec n)\vec n\right)\cdot\vec\sigma$: Rodrigues’ formula for a rotation by $\omega$ about $\vec n$ (check with $\vec n=\hat e_3$: $\hat e_1\to\cos\omega\,\hat e_1+\sin\omega\,\hat e_2$).
steps.explain: Multiply out $U\tilde xU^\dagger$ with the form from (ii) and use (i) to turn products of $\sigma$'s back into single $\sigma$'s. The half-angle products combine with double-angle formulas into $\cos\omega$ and $\sin\omega$. The coefficients are exactly Rodrigues' formula for a rotation by $\omega$ about $\vec n$: SU(2) acts on 3-vectors as rotations, two-to-one ($U$ and $-U$ give the same rotation).

enc.primer:
The question in plain words

A spin-$\frac12$ state is a vector in $\mathbb C^2$. If you rotate your lab, the spin state must change by some $2\times2$ unitary matrix. Which one rotates a spin by the angle $\omega$ about the axis $\vec n$? The answer is $U=e^{-i\frac\omega2\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma}$, with a surprising half angle that makes a full turn give $-1$.

The picture

The script’s trick: turn a vector into a matrix, $\tilde x=\vec x\cdot\vec\sigma=\begin{pmatrix}x_3&x_1-ix_2\\x_1+ix_2&-x_3\end{pmatrix}$ (7.71). It is hermitian and $\det\tilde x=-|\vec x|^2$ (7.73). Conjugating, $\tilde x\to U\tilde xU^\dagger$ keeps it hermitian and keeps the determinant: the length of $\vec x$ is preserved, so it is a rotation. Every SU(2) matrix gives a rotation, and $U$ and $-U$ give the same one: $SU(2)/\{\pm1\}\simeq SO(3)$ (7.76).

The pieces you need

  • Generators in the spin-$\frac12$ representation (7.85): $M_j=\sigma_j/2$, and rotations are exponentials of generators, like $R(\vec e_3,\varphi)=e^{-iM_3\varphi}$ (7.77).
  • Product rule: $\sigma_j\sigma_k=\delta_{jk}I+i\varepsilon_{jkl}\sigma_l$. Consequence: $(\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma)^2=I$ for a unit vector.
  • Because $(\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma)^2=I$, the exponential behaves like $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$: $U=\cos\frac\omega2\,I-i\sin\frac\omega2\,\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma$.
  • Full turn: $U(2\pi)=-I$ (7.78): half-integer spins pick up a sign; only $\pm$ pairs map to one rotation.

Tiny example

$\vec n=\vec e_3$: $U=\mathrm{diag}(e^{-i\omega/2},e^{i\omega/2})$. Then $U\sigma_1U^\dagger=\cos\omega\,\sigma_1+\sin\omega\,\sigma_2$: the vector $\vec e_1$ went to $\cos\omega\,\vec e_1+\sin\omega\,\vec e_2$, a rotation by $\omega$, although $U$ only contains $\omega/2$.

What this sheet question needs

(i) Multiply out the Pauli matrices (do $\sigma_1\sigma_2$ and $\sigma_1^2$, the rest is cyclic). (ii) Split the exponential series into even and odd powers using $(\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma)^2=I$. (iii) Compute $U\tilde xU^\dagger$: either for $\vec n=\vec e_3$ and argue by symmetry, or in general to get Rodrigues’ rotation formula.

Read in the script

§7.5 "SO(3) vs. SU(2)", pp. 75–77, eqs. (7.71)–(7.78); §7.7 "Der Spin des Elektrons", pp. 78–79, eq. (7.85) for $M_j=\sigma_j/2$. §7.6 (projective representations, p. 77) explains why the sign $-1$ is physically allowed.

enc.title: Sheet 9 Q8: 3D oscillator and su(3)

source.where: Exercise sheet IX, Question 4; official solution: Solutions 9.pdf

enc.goal: $H=\hbar\omega(a_1^\dagger a_1+a_2^\dagger a_2+a_3^\dagger a_3+\frac32)$. (i) Show $J_{ij}=a_i^\dagger a_j$ is conserved and $E_{ij}\mapsto J_{ij}$ is a Lie algebra isomorphism from u(3). (ii) For su(3) with $h_1=E_{11}-E_{22}$, $h_2=E_{22}-E_{33}$, $e_1=E_{12}$, $e_2=E_{23}$, $e_3=E_{13}$, $f_i=e_i^T$: compute $\mathrm{ad}_{h_i}$, the roots $\Delta_\pm$, and the su(2) subalgebras. (iii) Highest-weight theory of irreps. (iv) Show that the degenerate eigenspaces of $H$ are su(3) irreps and give their highest weight.

steps.reveal: $[H,a_i^\dagger a_j]=\hbar\omega(a_i^\dagger a_j-a_i^\dagger a_j)=0$. $[E_{ij},E_{kl}]=\delta_{jk}E_{il}-\delta_{il}E_{kj}$ and $[a_i^\dagger a_j,a_k^\dagger a_l]=\delta_{jk}a_i^\dagger a_l-\delta_{il}a_k^\dagger a_j$: the same bracket.
steps.explain: $a_i^\dagger a_j$ moves one quantum from direction $j$ to direction $i$: the total number, hence the energy, is unchanged, so it commutes with $H$. Its commutators reproduce those of the matrix units $E_{ij}$ (one use of $[a_j,a_k^\dagger]=\delta_{jk}$): the 9 operators form u(3).

steps.reveal: $[h_1,e_1]=2e_1$, $[h_2,e_1]=-e_1$: root $(2,-1)$; $e_2$: $(-1,2)$; $e_3$: $(1,1)$; the $f$’s have the negatives. Each positive root gives $\{e_\alpha,h_\alpha=[e_\alpha,f_\alpha],f_\alpha\}\cong$ su(2) (e.g. $e_3,h_1+h_2,f_3$).
steps.explain: Roots: the $h$'s are diagonal, so each $e$ is an eigenvector of "commutator with $h$"; the pair of eigenvalues is its root. E.g. $[E_{11}-E_{22},E_{12}]=2E_{12}$. Each root vector, its partner $f$ and their commutator form a copy of su(2), like $J_+,J_-,2J_3$.

steps.reveal: A finite irrep has a weight vector $v$ killed by all $e_\alpha$ (otherwise the weights would grow without bound); $V$ is spanned by the $f$’s acting on $v$. Restricting to each su(2) subalgebra forces $\lambda(h_\alpha)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. The adjoint rep has highest weight vector $e_3$, weight $(1,1)$.
steps.explain: Highest weight: raising operators $e$ increase the weight; in a finite-dimensional representation that must stop, so there is a vector killed by all $e$'s. Applying lowering operators to it generates the whole irrep. Inside each su(2) copy the weight must be a non-negative integer (spin-$j$ representations), which restricts the possible highest weights.

steps.reveal: Level $N$ = all $|n_1,n_2,n_3\rangle$ with $\sum n_i=N$, dimension $\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}{2}$. Highest weight vector $(a_1^\dagger)^N|0\rangle$, weight $(N,0)$: the symmetric irrep $\mathrm{Sym}^N(\mathbb C^3)$; su(3) explains the full degeneracy (more than SO(3) alone).
steps.explain: Level $N$ holds all ways to distribute $N$ quanta in 3 directions, $\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}{2}$ states (sheet 7 Q3). The $J$'s map this level to itself. The state with all quanta in direction 1 cannot be raised further (there is nowhere "higher" to move a quantum): it is the highest weight, $(N,0)$. Its irrep has exactly that dimension, so the whole level is one su(3) irrep: su(3) explains the full degeneracy.

enc.primer:
The question in plain words

The 3D oscillator level $N$ has $\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}2$ states: 1, 3, 6, 10, ... Rotations alone cannot explain this: an irreducible rotation multiplet $D_l$ has only $2l+1$ states, and one level contains several of them ($l=N,N-2,\dots$). Whenever states share an energy "by accident", look for a bigger symmetry. Here it is su(3).

The picture

Picture the $N$ energy quanta as $N$ identical balls in three boxes labelled $x,y,z$. The energy only counts the balls, not which box they are in. The operator $a_i^\dagger a_j$ takes a ball from box $j$ and puts it into box $i$: it changes the state but not the energy. All these "ball movers" commute with $H$, and together they form a symmetry algebra bigger than rotations.

The pieces you need

  • The 9 operators $J_{ij}=a_i^\dagger a_j$ obey the same brackets as the $3\times3$ matrix units $E_{ij}$: u(3). The trace part $\sum_iJ_{ii}=N$ just counts; the rest is su(3).
  • Strategy from §7.4 for so(3): find a vector killed by the raising operator ($M_+\psi_j=0$, (7.37)), then get everything by lowering; finite dimension forces $j$ to be half-integer (7.43).
  • New for su(3): two commuting "$M_3$"s ($h_1,h_2$), so weights are pairs $(m,n)$, and three raising operators $e_1,e_2,e_3$. A highest weight vector is killed by all three.
  • Each raising operator, its lowering partner and their commutator form a copy of su(2). Inside each copy the §7.4 argument applies: that is why the weights must be integers.

Tiny example

Level $N=1$: the three states $a_1^\dagger|0\rangle,a_2^\dagger|0\rangle,a_3^\dagger|0\rangle$. The ball movers shuffle them like the components of a vector in $\mathbb C^3$: the fundamental representation of su(3). Highest weight: $a_1^\dagger|0\rangle$, weight $(1,0)$. For level $N$: $(a_1^\dagger)^N|0\rangle$, weight $(N,0)$, dimension $\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}2$.

What this sheet question needs

(i) $[H,a_i^\dagger a_j]=0$ and matching brackets with $E_{ij}$. (ii) Compute $[h_i,\cdot]$ on the $e$’s and $f$’s: the eigenvalues are the roots. (iii) Repeat the §7.4 argument with three raising operators. (iv) Identify the oscillator level $N$ as the representation with highest weight $(N,0)$. Warm-ups: sheet 7 Q3 (counting the states) and sheet 8 Q3 (the same idea with su(2) in 2D).

enc.goal: $H=\frac{\vec p^2}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}\vec x^2$. (i) Spectrum and degeneracies from what you know. (ii) With $\Psi=\frac{u(r)}rY_{\ell m}$, $-u^{\prime\prime}+\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}u+\frac{m^2\omega^2}{\hbar^2}r^2u=\varepsilon u$, $\varepsilon=\frac{2mE}{\hbar^2}$: show $u\sim r^{\ell+1}$ ($r\to0$) and $u\sim e^{-m\omega r^2/2\hbar}$ ($r\to\infty$); contrast with hydrogen. (iii) With $u=e^{-m\omega r^2/2\hbar}\sum_{k\ge\ell+1}c_kr^k$ derive $c_{k+2}=\frac{\frac{m\omega}\hbar(2k+1)-\varepsilon}{(k+2)(k+1)-\ell(\ell+1)}c_k$; which $c_k$ vanish, how many are free? (iv) Square integrability: allowed energies at fixed $\ell$; draw the $(\ell,E)$ spectrum. (v) Recover (i).

steps.reveal: $E=\hbar\omega(N+\frac32)$, degeneracy $\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}2$ (sheet VII Q3).
steps.explain: In Cartesian coordinates the 3D oscillator is three independent 1D oscillators: $E=\hbar\omega(n_x+n_y+n_z+\frac32)$, and the degeneracy is the number of ways to split $N$ into three, $\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}{2}$ (sheet 7 Q3). This is the answer the spherical calculation must reproduce.

steps.reveal: $r\to0$: $u^{\prime\prime}\approx\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}u$, $u=r^{\ell+1}$ or $r^{-\ell}$; the second is not square integrable (or, for $\ell=0$, would need a $\delta$ potential). $r\to\infty$: $u=e^S$, $S^{\prime2}\approx\alpha^2r^2$, $S=-\alpha r^2/2$ ($\alpha=m\omega/\hbar$). Hydrogen decays only like $e^{-\kappa r}$; here the confining $r^2$ potential gives a Gaussian and no scattering states: the whole spectrum is discrete.
steps.explain: Asymptotic analysis: near $r=0$ the centrifugal term $\ell(\ell+1)/r^2$ dominates everything else, so solve only $u''=\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}u$: powers $r^{\ell+1}$ and $r^{-\ell}$; only the first is acceptable. For $r\to\infty$ the $r^2$ term dominates; try $u=e^S$: $S'^2\approx\alpha^2r^2$ gives a Gaussian. A confining potential that grows forever has no scattering states.

steps.reveal: Insert $u=e^{-\alpha r^2/2}f$: $-f^{\prime\prime}+\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}f+2\alpha rf^\prime+(\alpha-\varepsilon)f=0$; equate powers of $r$: the stated recursion. Starting from $c_{\ell+1}$ in steps of 2, all $c_k$ with $k-\ell$ even vanish; only $c_{\ell+1}$ is free (normalisation).
steps.explain: Peel off the known behaviour ($u=e^{-\alpha r^2/2}f$) and expand the rest in powers of $r$. Inserting and collecting the coefficient of each power gives a two-step recursion: $c_{k+2}$ from $c_k$. Starting at $c_{\ell+1}$ only every second power appears, so one free constant.

steps.reveal: If the series does not stop, $c_{k+2}/c_k\to2\alpha/k$ and $f\sim e^{\alpha r^2}$: not normalisable. It stops at $k_{\max}=\ell+1+2n_r$ iff $\varepsilon=\alpha(2k_{\max}+1)$, i.e. $E=\hbar\omega\left(2n_r+\ell+\frac32\right)$. In the $(\ell,E)$ plane: at $E=\hbar\omega(N+\frac32)$ the allowed $\ell=N,N-2,\dots,1$ or 0.
steps.explain: The series must stop. For large $k$ the ratio $c_{k+2}/c_k\approx2\alpha/k$ is that of $e^{\alpha r^2}$, which would overwhelm the Gaussian and make $u$ blow up. It stops only if the numerator vanishes at some $k_{\max}$: $\varepsilon=\alpha(2k_{\max}+1)$, which is the quantisation of $E$. Writing $k_{\max}=\ell+1+2n_r$ ($n_r$ = number of radial nodes) gives $E=\hbar\omega(2n_r+\ell+\frac32)$.

steps.reveal: $\sum_{\ell=N,N-2,\dots}(2\ell+1)=\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}{2}$: agrees with (i). Same $N$ for different $\ell$: an accidental degeneracy, explained by the hidden su(3) (sheet IX Q4).
steps.explain: At $N=2n_r+\ell$ the allowed $\ell$ are $N,N-2,\dots$; each $\ell$ has $2\ell+1$ values of $m$. Summing $(2\ell+1)$ over these $\ell$ gives back $\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}{2}$. Different $\ell$ having the same energy is not explained by rotations alone: it is the hidden su(3) of sheet 9 Q4.

enc.title: Sheet 10 Q2: Projective representations of Z2 x Z2

source.where: Exercise sheet X, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 10.pdf

enc.goal: $G=\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2$ with generators $g,h$: $g^2=h^2=\mathrm{id}$, $gh=hg$. (i) Show that $\gamma(\mathrm{id})=\mathbb 1$, $\gamma(g)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $\gamma(h)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\gamma(gh)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is a projective representation, $\gamma(a)\gamma(b)=c_2(a,b)\gamma(ab)$, with $c_2(a,b)=+1$ if $a=\mathrm{id}$ or $b=\mathrm{id}$ or $a=h$ or $b=g$, else $-1$. (ii) Show that no 1-cycle $c_1(a)$ makes $\hat c_2(a,b)=c_2(a,b)\frac{c_1(a)c_1(b)}{c_1(ab)}=+1$ for all pairs. (iii) $E=\mathbb Z_2\times G$ with $(x,a)\cdot(y,b)=(xy\,c_2(a,b),ab)$: show $E$ is a group (isomorphic to $D_4$) and $\hat\gamma(\pm1,a)=\pm\gamma(a)$ is an honest representation. (iv) General $G$, projective $\rho$ with phases $c_2$, $U\subset U(1)$ generated by them: $E=U\times G$ with $(u_1,g)(u_2,h)=(u_1u_2c_2(g,h),gh)$ is a group and $\hat\rho(u,g)=u\rho(g)$ is an honest representation.
given: Due Monday 23.11.2026 (sheet X of this year). The lecturer’s chapter 7 explainer pack has a page on projective representations.

steps.reveal: Products with $\mathrm{id}$ are trivial ($c_2=+1$). Squares: $\gamma(g)^2=\gamma(h)^2=\mathbb 1$ but $\gamma(gh)^2=-\mathbb 1$, so $c_2(gh,gh)=-1$. Mixed: $\gamma(h)\gamma(g)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=+\gamma(gh)$, while $\gamma(g)\gamma(h)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=-\gamma(gh)$; likewise $\gamma(g)\gamma(gh)=-\gamma(h)$, $\gamma(gh)\gamma(h)=-\gamma(g)$, $\gamma(h)\gamma(gh)=+\gamma(g)$, $\gamma(gh)\gamma(g)=+\gamma(h)$. The four minus signs are exactly $(g,h),(g,gh),(gh,h),(gh,gh)$: the pairs with $a\notin\{\mathrm{id},h\}$ and $b\notin\{\mathrm{id},g\}$, as stated.
steps.explain: What to check: for every pair $(a,b)$ multiply the two matrices and compare with $\gamma(ab)$; the sign that appears is $c_2(a,b)$. Products with the identity are trivial. The interesting fact: $\gamma(g)\gamma(h)=-\gamma(h)\gamma(g)$, the matrices anticommute although $g$ and $h$ commute in the group, so one order must carry a $-1$.

steps.prompt: (ii) A phase no rephasing can kill.
steps.reveal: Since $G$ is abelian, $gh=hg$, so $\frac{\hat c_2(g,h)}{\hat c_2(h,g)}=\frac{c_2(g,h)}{c_2(h,g)}\cdot\frac{c_1(g)c_1(h)/c_1(gh)}{c_1(h)c_1(g)/c_1(hg)}=\frac{c_2(g,h)}{c_2(h,g)}=\frac{-1}{+1}=-1$ for any $c_1$. Both cannot be $+1$. Physically: $\gamma(g)$ and $\gamma(h)$ anticommute, and rescaling matrices by phases never turns anticommuting into commuting, whereas an honest rep of an abelian group has commuting images.
steps.explain: Why no rephasing helps: look at the ratio $c_2(g,h)/c_2(h,g)$. Rephasing $\gamma(a)\to c_1(a)\gamma(a)$ changes $c_2(g,h)$ and $c_2(h,g)$ by the same factor (because $gh=hg$), so the ratio is invariant, and it equals $-1$. Matrices that anticommute stay anticommuting after multiplying them by numbers; an honest representation of an abelian group would need commuting matrices.

steps.reveal: Closure is clear; identity $(1,\mathrm{id})$; inverse of $(x,a)$ is $(x\,c_2(a,a),a)$ since $a^{-1}=a$ and $c_2=\pm1$. Associativity needs the cocycle condition $c_2(a,b)c_2(ab,c)=c_2(b,c)c_2(a,bc)$, which follows from $(\gamma(a)\gamma(b))\gamma(c)=\gamma(a)(\gamma(b)\gamma(c))$ and invertibility of $\gamma(abc)$. Homomorphism: $\hat\gamma(x,a)\hat\gamma(y,b)=xy\,\gamma(a)\gamma(b)=xy\,c_2(a,b)\gamma(ab)=\hat\gamma\big((x,a)(y,b)\big)$. The 8 matrices $\pm\gamma(a)$ are distinct, so $\hat\gamma$ is faithful and $E\cong\{\pm\mathbb 1,\pm\gamma(g),\pm\gamma(h),\pm\gamma(gh)\}$: $\gamma(gh)$ is the rotation by $90^\circ$ (order 4), $\gamma(g)$ a reflection, together the symmetry group of a square, $D_4$ (order 8, non-abelian).
steps.explain: The fix: make the sign part of the group element. Pairs (sign, group element) with the product rule twisted by $c_2$ form a bigger group $E$ of 8 elements, and $\pm\gamma(a)$ represent it honestly. Associativity of $E$ is inherited from associativity of matrix multiplication (the cocycle condition). The 8 matrices are the symmetries of a square: $D_4$.

steps.reveal: Identical proof: $U$ is an abelian group of phases, so closure holds; the identity is $(1,e)$ with $c_2(e,g)=c_2(g,e)=1$ (choose $\rho(e)=\mathbb 1$); the inverse of $(u,g)$ is $(u^{-1}c_2(g,g^{-1})^{-1},g^{-1})$; associativity is again the cocycle condition from associativity of $\rho$. $\hat\rho(u_1,g)\hat\rho(u_2,h)=u_1u_2\rho(g)\rho(h)=u_1u_2c_2(g,h)\rho(gh)=\hat\rho\big((u_1,g)(u_2,h)\big)$. For SO(3) the phases of the spin-$\frac12$ rep are $\pm1$ ($R(2\pi)=-\mathbb 1$), so $U=\mathbb Z_2$ and $E$ is the double cover SU(2).
steps.explain: The same construction works for any group: collect all phases that appear into an abelian group $U$, and let the pairs $(u,g)$ multiply with the twist. This is how spin $\frac12$ works: SO(3) has only a projective representation on spinors (a $2\pi$ rotation gives $-1$), and the "bigger group" is SU(2), the double cover.

keyPoints: SO(3) $\to$ SU(2) as the $\mathbb Z_2$ cover

enc.title: Sheet 11 Q1: More on the dynamical symmetry

source.where: Exercise sheet XI, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 11.pdf

enc.goal: Pauli-Lenz vector $\vec J=\frac1{2m}(\vec p\wedge\vec L-\vec L\wedge\vec p)-\kappa\frac{\vec x}r$; on a fixed negative energy $\vec S=\frac12(\vec L+a\vec J)$, $\vec D=\frac12(\vec L-a\vec J)$ form su(2) $\oplus$ su(2). (i) The highest weight vector $|\psi\rangle$ (killed by $S_+$, $D_+$) satisfies $J_+|\psi\rangle=L_+|\psi\rangle=0$, so it is a superposition of $|n,l,l\rangle$. (ii) Compute $[L_\pm,J_+]$, $[L_3,J_+]$; show $J_+|n,l,l\rangle\propto|n,l+1,l+1\rangle$ and $|\psi\rangle=|n,n-1,n-1\rangle$. (iii) Check explicitly: $\psi\propto r^{n-1}\sin^{n-1}\theta\,e^{i(n-1)\varphi}e^{-m\kappa r/\hbar^2n}$ and $J_+\psi=0$. (v) Describe the eigenspace with ladder operators and count its dimension.

steps.reveal: $S_+\pm$ and $D_+$ combinations: $S_+|\psi\rangle=D_+|\psi\rangle=0\Leftrightarrow L_+|\psi\rangle=0$ and $J_+|\psi\rangle=0$. $L_+|\psi\rangle=0$ means $m=l$ in each $l$ component: $|\psi\rangle=\sum_lc_l|n,l,l\rangle$.
steps.explain: $S$ and $D$ are combinations of $L$ and $J$, so "killed by $S_+$ and $D_+$" is equivalent to "killed by $L_+$ and $J_+$" (add and subtract). A state killed by $L_+$ has the maximal $m=l$ in each angular-momentum component, so it is a sum of states $|n,l,l\rangle$.

steps.reveal: From $[L_j,J_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}J_l$: $[L_+,J_+]=0$, $[L_3,J_+]=\hbar J_+$, $[L_-,J_+]=-2\hbar J_3$. So $J_+|n,l,l\rangle$ has $L_3=\hbar(l+1)$ and is killed by $L_+$: it is a highest weight of spin $l+1$, $\propto|n,l+1,l+1\rangle$. Then $J_+|\psi\rangle=0$ forces $c_l=0$ unless $l$ is maximal: $|\psi\rangle=|n,n-1,n-1\rangle$.
steps.explain: $J$ is a vector operator: $[L_j,J_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}J_l$, so $J_+$ behaves like a "raising" vector: it adds $\hbar$ to $L_3$ and commutes with $L_+$. Applied to $|n,l,l\rangle$ it therefore gives a state with $m=l+1$ still killed by $L_+$, i.e. $\propto|n,l+1,l+1\rangle$. If $J_+$ must kill the whole sum, each term must be killed, which only happens at the top value $l=n-1$ (there is no $l=n$).

steps.reveal: For $l=n-1$, $u_{n,n-1}\propto r^ne^{-r/na_0}$ (no radial nodes) and $Y_{n-1,n-1}\propto\sin^{n-1}\theta e^{i(n-1)\varphi}$, giving the stated $\psi$ with $\frac{m\kappa}{\hbar^2}=\frac1{a_0}$. With $J_+=\frac im(p_3L_+-\hbar p_+-p_+L_3)-\kappa\sin\theta e^{i\varphi}$ and the given $p_+$, $L_+\psi=0$, $L_3\psi=\hbar(n-1)\psi$, the remaining terms cancel: $J_+\psi=0$.
steps.explain: Explicit check: the state with $l=n-1$, $m=n-1$ has no radial nodes and the angular part $\sin^{n-1}\theta\,e^{i(n-1)\varphi}$ (the top spherical harmonic). Acting with the explicit $J_+$ operator, the terms cancel. This confirms the algebraic argument.

steps.reveal: $|\psi\rangle$ has $S_3=D_3=\frac{n-1}2$: spin $j=\frac{n-1}2$ for both su(2)s. The eigenspace is spanned by $S_-^aD_-^b|\psi\rangle$, $0\le a,b\le n-1$: dimension $(2j+1)^2=n^2$.
steps.explain: Counting: $|\psi\rangle$ is the top state of two spins, each with $j=\frac{n-1}{2}$. Lowering independently with $S_-$ and $D_-$ gives $(2j+1)\times(2j+1)=n^2$ states: the full degeneracy of the hydrogen level $n$, explained by symmetry.

enc.title: Sheet 11 Q2: Spinors

source.where: Exercise sheet XI, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 11.pdf

enc.goal: (i) A spin-$\frac12$ state has $\langle\vec\sigma\rangle=\vec e$ (unit vector). Find $|\chi\rangle$. (ii) Probability that $S_z$ gives $+\hbar/2$?

steps.reveal: With $\vec e=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$: $|\chi\rangle=\binom{\cos\frac\theta2}{e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac\theta2}$ (up to a phase), the $+1$ eigenvector of $\vec e\cdot\vec\sigma$; check $\langle\sigma_3\rangle=\cos^2\frac\theta2-\sin^2\frac\theta2=\cos\theta$.
steps.explain: A spin-½ state "points" somewhere: the state with $\langle\vec\sigma\rangle=\vec e$ is the $+1$ eigenvector of $\vec e\cdot\vec\sigma$ (spin up along $\vec e$). Solving the $2\times2$ eigenproblem with $\vec e$ in spherical angles gives $(\cos\frac\theta2,e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac\theta2)$. Half angles again: the Bloch sphere angle $\theta$ is twice the "mixing angle" in Hilbert space.

steps.reveal: $P(S_z=+\frac\hbar2)=\cos^2\frac\theta2=\frac{1+e_z}{2}$.
steps.explain: $P(\uparrow_z)=|\langle\uparrow|\chi\rangle|^2=\cos^2\frac\theta2=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}$. Checks: along $+z$ certainty, along $-z$ zero, in the equator 50/50.

enc.title: Sheet 11 Q3: Addition of spins

source.where: Exercise sheet XI, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 11.pdf

enc.goal: Decompose $D_{1/2}\otimes D_1$ into irreducible representations.

steps.reveal: Dimension $2\times3=6$; total $m$ ranges over $\pm\frac32,\pm\frac12$ with multiplicities $1,2$: $D_{1/2}\otimes D_1=D_{3/2}\oplus D_{1/2}$ ($4+2=6$), as the Clebsch-Gordan series $|j_1-j_2|\le j\le j_1+j_2$ says.
steps.explain: Counting method: list the possible total $m=m_1+m_2$ with their multiplicities. The largest, $\frac32$, occurs once and must start a $j=\frac32$ multiplet (4 states). Remove those; what remains has top $m=\frac12$, so a $j=\frac12$ multiplet. $4+2=6$ states, all accounted for. General rule: $j$ runs from $|j_1-j_2|$ to $j_1+j_2$ in steps of 1.

enc.title: Sheet 12 Q1: Stern-Gerlach experiment

source.where: Exercise sheet XII, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 12.pdf

enc.goal: Sketch the screen of Stern-Gerlach experiments with molecules made of (i) two spin-$\frac12$ atoms, (ii) three spin-$\frac12$ atoms.

steps.reveal: $D_{1/2}\otimes D_{1/2}=D_1\oplus D_0$; the deflection measures total $m$: three spots $m=+1,0,-1$, intensities $1:2:1$ for unpolarised molecules (the middle spot holds $m=0$ of the triplet and the singlet).
steps.explain: What the magnet measures: the deflection is proportional to the total $m$ of the molecule. Two spins ½ combine into a triplet ($m=1,0,-1$) and a singlet ($m=0$). Unpolarised: each of the 4 product states is equally likely; $m=0$ occurs twice ($\uparrow\downarrow,\downarrow\uparrow$), so the middle spot gets twice the intensity.

steps.reveal: $D_{1/2}^{\otimes3}=D_{3/2}\oplus2D_{1/2}$: four spots $m=\pm\frac32,\pm\frac12$ with intensities $1:3:3:1$ (an even number of spots: half-integer total spin).
steps.explain: Three spins: count the $2^3=8$ product states by $m$: $m=\frac32$ once, $\frac12$ three times, $-\frac12$ three times, $-\frac32$ once. Four spots with $1:3:3:1$ (binomial coefficients).

enc.title: Sheet 12 Q2: Vectors and tensors

source.where: Exercise sheet XII, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 12.pdf

enc.goal: (i) Show that the so(3) representation of the defining SO(3) action is spin 1 ($M_j=i\frac{d}{d\varphi}R_j(\varphi)|_0$). (ii) Show that $\vec x$ and $\vec p$ transform as vectors under $O\mapsto\hbar^{-1}[L_j,O]$. (iii) Highest and lowest weight components of a vector (spherical basis). (iv) Decompose $S^2D_1$. (v) Combine two vectors $\vec J,\vec K$ symmetrically into a scalar $S$ and a tensor $T$.

steps.reveal: $(M_j)_{kl}=-i\varepsilon_{jkl}$; $M_3$ has eigenvalues $-1,0,1$ and $\vec M^2=2=1(1+1)$: the 3-dimensional irrep $D_1$.
steps.explain: The generators of rotations of 3-vectors are $3\times3$ matrices with entries $\pm1$ from $\varepsilon$. Computing $\vec M^2$ gives $2\cdot I=1(1+1)$, and $M_3$ has eigenvalues $-1,0,1$: by definition this is spin 1. "A vector is spin 1."

steps.reveal: $[L_j,x_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}x_l$, $[L_j,p_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}p_l$: exactly the action of $M_j$ (up to the factor $i$ convention): vector operators.
steps.explain: Vector operator means: commuting with $L_j$ rotates its components exactly like a vector, $[L_j,V_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}V_l$. For $\vec x$ and $\vec p$ this follows from $[x,p]=i\hbar$ and $\vec L=\vec x\times\vec p$.

steps.reveal: $J_{\pm1}=\mp\frac1{\sqrt2}(J_1\pm iJ_2)$, $J_0=J_3$: $J_{+1}$ is highest weight ($[L_+,J_{+1}]=0$), $J_{-1}$ lowest.
steps.explain: The spherical components $V_{\pm1}=\mp\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(V_1\pm iV_2)$, $V_0=V_3$ are the analogue of $|1,\pm1\rangle$, $|1,0\rangle$. $V_{+1}$ is "highest": raising it further gives zero.

steps.reveal: $S^2D_1$ has dimension 6 $=D_2\oplus D_0$ (a tensor and a scalar; the antisymmetric part would be $D_1$). Scalar $S=\vec J\cdot\vec K$; tensor $T_{ij}=\frac12(J_iK_j+J_jK_i)-\frac13\delta_{ij}\vec J\cdot\vec K$ (symmetric, traceless: 5 components).
steps.explain: Dimension count: symmetric products of two 3-vectors: $3\cdot4/2=6$ components. A scalar (the dot product, 1 component) can always be split off; the rest is a symmetric traceless tensor with 5 components, i.e. spin 2. So $6=5+1$. (The antisymmetric part, the cross product, would be the remaining spin 1.)

enc.title: Sheet 12 Q3: Clebsch-Gordan coefficients

source.where: Exercise sheet XII, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 12.pdf

enc.goal: (i) Prove $\langle l,\frac12,m\mp\frac12,\pm\frac12|l,\frac12,l+\frac12,m\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{l\pm m+\frac12}{2l+1}}$. (ii) For $l=1$ write the states $|j=\frac32,j_z\rangle$ in terms of $|m,s\rangle$.

steps.reveal: $|l+\frac12,l+\frac12\rangle=|l,\uparrow\rangle$ (coefficient 1). Apply $J_-=L_-+S_-$ repeatedly; the recursion relates neighbouring coefficients, $\frac{c(m-1)}{c(m)}=\sqrt{\frac{l+m-\frac12}{l+m+\frac12}}$ for the $\uparrow$ part, which telescopes to $\sqrt{\frac{l+m+\frac12}{2l+1}}$; normalisation (or the other recursion) gives the $\downarrow$ coefficient $\sqrt{\frac{l-m+\frac12}{2l+1}}$.
steps.explain: Start at the top, where there is only one way: $|j=l+\frac12,m=l+\frac12\rangle=|l,\uparrow\rangle$. Apply $J_-=L_-+S_-$ to both sides: the left gives the next $|j,m\rangle$ with a known factor, the right gives a combination of $|l-1,\uparrow\rangle$ and $|l,\downarrow\rangle$ with known factors. Repeating gives a recursion between neighbouring coefficients; the ratios telescope (multiply out) to the closed formula.

steps.reveal: $|\frac32,\frac32\rangle=|1,\uparrow\rangle$, $|\frac32,\frac12\rangle=\sqrt{\frac23}|0,\uparrow\rangle+\sqrt{\frac13}|1,\downarrow\rangle$, $|\frac32,-\frac12\rangle=\sqrt{\frac13}|-1,\uparrow\rangle+\sqrt{\frac23}|0,\downarrow\rangle$, $|\frac32,-\frac32\rangle=|-1,\downarrow\rangle$ (the $j=\frac12$ states are the orthogonal combinations).
steps.explain: For $l=1$ just apply the formula with $m=\frac12$ and $m=-\frac12$, or lower once from the top by hand. The $j=\frac12$ states are the orthogonal combinations of the same two basis states.

enc.title: Sheet 13 Q1: Time-energy uncertainty

source.where: Exercise sheet XIII, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 13.pdf

enc.goal: (i) Show $\langle\psi|\psi(t)\rangle=\exp\left[-\frac{it}\hbar\langle H\rangle-\frac{t^2}{2\hbar^2}(\Delta H)^2\right](1+O(|t|^3))$. (ii) Show $P[\text{no change}]=\exp(-(\Delta H)^2t^2/\hbar^2)(1+O(|t|^3))$. (iii) What if $|\psi\rangle$ is an eigenstate of $H$?

steps.reveal: $\langle\psi|e^{-iHt/\hbar}|\psi\rangle=1-\frac{it}\hbar\langle H\rangle-\frac{t^2}{2\hbar^2}\langle H^2\rangle+O(t^3)$; the exponential gives the same with $\langle H^2\rangle=(\Delta H)^2+\langle H\rangle^2$.
steps.explain: Expand both sides to second order in $t$. Left: the exponential $e^{-iHt/\hbar}$ to second order, sandwiched in $|\psi\rangle$, gives $1-\frac{it}{\hbar}\langle H\rangle-\frac{t^2}{2\hbar^2}\langle H^2\rangle$. Right: expand the claimed exponential; its $t^2$ term has $(\Delta H)^2+\langle H\rangle^2=\langle H^2\rangle$. Same to order $t^2$.

steps.reveal: $|\langle\psi|\psi(t)\rangle|^2$: the phase drops out, $e^{-(\Delta H)^2t^2/\hbar^2}$: the decay time is $\sim\hbar/\Delta H$. For an eigenstate $P=1$ for all $t$, consistent since $\Delta H=0$.
steps.explain: The probability is the modulus squared: the first term is a pure phase and drops out, the Gaussian factor squares. So the state starts to change on the time scale $\hbar/\Delta H$: a large energy spread means fast change. An energy eigenstate has $\Delta H=0$ and never changes (apart from a phase).

enc.title: Sheet 13 Q2: Quantum Zeno effect

source.where: Exercise sheet XIII, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 13.pdf

enc.goal: $U_t=e^{-iHt/\hbar}$, $P=|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|$. (i) Show $PU_{t/n}P\cdots U_{t/n}P=\langle\phi|U_{t/n}|\phi\rangle^nP$. (ii) Show $\langle\phi|U_{t/n}|\phi\rangle^n=e^{-i\langle H\rangle t/\hbar}(1+O(t^2/n))$. (iii) Deduce the limit $n\to\infty$ and interpret.

steps.reveal: Each $P\,U\,P=|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|U|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|$: $n$ numbers $\langle\phi|U_{t/n}|\phi\rangle$ times $P$.
steps.explain: Between measurements the state evolves with $U$; each measurement projects back onto $|\phi\rangle$. In $PUP=|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|U|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|$ the middle is just a number. A chain of $n$ such blocks is that number to the power $n$, times $P$.

steps.reveal: By Q1, $\langle\phi|U_{t/n}|\phi\rangle=e^{-i\langle H\rangle t/n\hbar}(1+O(t^2/n^2))$; to the power $n$: $(1+O(t^2/n^2))^n=1+O(t^2/n)\to1$. So the limit is $e^{-i\langle H\rangle t/\hbar}P$: continuous measurement freezes the state (watched pot).
steps.explain: Why the limit freezes the state. By Q1 the survival amplitude over a short time $\tau$ deviates from a phase only at order $\tau^2$. With $\tau=t/n$, $n$ factors of $(1-O(t^2/n^2))$ give $1-O(t^2/n)\to1$. The loss per step is quadratic, but the number of steps only linear, so frequent enough measurement stops the evolution: the quantum Zeno effect.

enc.title: Sheet 13 Q3: Hardy’s paradox

source.where: Exercise sheet XIII, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 13.pdf

enc.goal: $|\psi\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt3}(|++\rangle+|-+\rangle+|--\rangle)$. Alice measures $A_0$ (basis $|\pm\rangle$) or $A_1$ (basis $|\pm\hat n\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt2}(|+\rangle\pm|-\rangle)$), Bob $B_0$ ($|\pm\rangle$) or $B_1$ ($|+\hat m\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt5}(2|+\rangle+|-\rangle)$, $|-\hat m\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt5}(|+\rangle-2|-\rangle)$). (i) Show $|\psi\rangle\propto|+\hat n\rangle(2|+\rangle+|-\rangle)-|-\hat n\rangle|-\rangle$. (ii) Show $P[a_0>b_0]=P[b_0>a_1]=P[a_1>b_1]=0$. (iii) Classically that implies $P[a_0>b_1]=0$. (iv) Show quantum mechanically $P[a_0>b_1]>0$.

steps.reveal: $|\pm\rangle$ in terms of $|\pm\hat n\rangle$: $|\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\left[|+\hat n\rangle(2|+\rangle+|-\rangle)-|-\hat n\rangle|-\rangle\right]$.
steps.explain: Express $|+\rangle$ and $|-\rangle$ for Alice through $|\pm\hat n\rangle$: $|\pm\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt2}(|+\hat n\rangle\pm|-\hat n\rangle)$. Insert, collect the terms with $|+\hat n\rangle$ and with $|-\hat n\rangle$. Writing a state "in the basis of the measurement" shows directly what the other side is left with after each result.

steps.reveal: $a_0=+1$ leaves $|++\rangle$: $b_0=+1$ surely. $a_1=-1$ leaves $|-\hat n\rangle|-\rangle$: $b_0=-1$ surely. $a_1=+1$ leaves $|+\hat n\rangle\propto|+\hat n\rangle|+\hat m\rangle$: $b_1=+1$ surely.
steps.explain: Read off from the different ways of writing $|\psi\rangle$: after each specified result of one side, the other side is left in a definite state, so its result is certain. E.g. $a_0=+1$: only the $|++\rangle$ term has Alice $+$, so Bob's $b_0$ is $+1$. These certain correlations are the three "zeros".

steps.reveal: Classically $a_0\le b_0\le a_1\le b_1$ always, so $a_0\le b_1$. Quantum: $a_0=+1$ (probability $\frac13$) leaves $|+\rangle$ for Bob, and $|\langle-\hat m|+\rangle|^2=\frac15$: $P[a_0>b_1]=\frac1{15}>0$. The values of non-commuting observables cannot all exist at once (no joint distribution).
steps.explain: The paradox: if all four values existed simultaneously, the three certainties would chain together and forbid $a_0=+1$, $b_1=-1$. Quantum mechanically: $a_0=+1$ with probability $\frac13$, then Bob has $|+\rangle$, and $|\langle-\hat m|+\rangle|^2=\frac15$. So the "impossible" event happens with probability $\frac1{15}$: the values of incompatible observables do not exist before measurement.

keyPoints: post-measurement states for the three zeros

sheets.title: Perturbation theory: anharmonic, Stark, spin-orbit and Zeeman

enc.title: Sheet 14 Q1: Anharmonic oscillator

source.where: Exercise sheet XIV, Question 1; official solution: Solutions 14.pdf

enc.goal: $H=H_0+\lambda(x/x_0)^4$, $x_0=\sqrt{\hbar/m\omega}$. (i) Write $H$ with $a,a^\dagger$. (ii) Matrix elements of $H_a$ and the first-order shift. (iii) Energies to second order in $\lambda$. (iv) Why does perturbation theory fail for large $n$?

steps.reveal: $x/x_0=(a+a^\dagger)/\sqrt2$: $H=\hbar\omega(a^\dagger a+\frac12)+\frac\lambda4(a+a^\dagger)^4$.
steps.explain: Express $x$ with ladder operators, $x=x_0\frac{a+a^\dagger}{\sqrt2}$; then $(x/x_0)^4=\frac14(a+a^\dagger)^4$. Everything is now in the language where matrix elements are easy.

steps.reveal: Non-zero: $\langle n\pm4|$, $\langle n\pm2|$, $\langle n|$. Normal ordering gives $\langle n|(a+a^\dagger)^4|n\rangle=6n^2+6n+3$: $E^{(1)}_n=\frac{3\lambda}4(2n^2+2n+1)$.
steps.explain: Which elements survive: $(a+a^\dagger)^4$ is a sum of 16 products of four ladder operators, each changing $n$ by $\pm1$, so the net change is $0,\pm2,\pm4$. First order needs only the diagonal one: count the products with two $a$ and two $a^\dagger$ and evaluate them on $|n\rangle$; they add up to $6n^2+6n+3$.

steps.reveal: $E_n^{(2)}=\sum_{k=\pm2,\pm4}\frac{|\langle n+k|H_a|n\rangle|^2}{-k\hbar\omega}=-\frac{\lambda^2}{8\hbar\omega}(34n^3+51n^2+59n+21)$; ground state $E_0=\hbar\omega\left[\frac12+\frac34\frac{\lambda}{\hbar\omega}-\frac{21}8\left(\frac{\lambda}{\hbar\omega}\right)^2\right]$.
steps.explain: Second order formula $E^{(2)}_n=\sum_{k\ne n}\frac{|\langle k|H_a|n\rangle|^2}{E_n-E_k}$: here $k=n\pm2,n\pm4$ with denominators $\mp2\hbar\omega,\mp4\hbar\omega$. The ground state has only $k=2,4$ (no levels below), both making the energy lower: second order always lowers the ground state.

steps.reveal: $E^{(1)}_n/E^{(0)}_n\sim\frac{3\lambda n}{\hbar\omega}$ grows: at large amplitudes $x^4$ dominates $x^2$, so it is no longer a small perturbation (and the series is only asymptotic: for $\lambda<0$ the potential is unbounded).
steps.explain: Small compared to what? The correction must be small compared with the level spacing $\hbar\omega$. But $E^{(1)}_n$ grows like $n^2$: for large $n$ the particle swings far out where $x^4$ beats $x^2$, and the "perturbation" dominates. Perturbation theory is a small-amplitude expansion.

enc.title: Sheet 14 Q2: Stark effect

source.where: Exercise sheet XIV, Question 2; official solution: Solutions 14.pdf

enc.goal: Hydrogen in a field $\vec E$: $\Delta H=-e\vec E\cdot\vec x$ ($e<0$). Use degenerate perturbation theory for $n=2$: energy shifts and eigenstates to first order.

steps.reveal: Take $\vec E=E\hat z$, $\Delta H=-eEz$. $z$ is odd (parity) and commutes with $L_z$: only $\langle200|z|210\rangle$ survives in the 4-dimensional $n=2$ space.
steps.explain: Before computing, use symmetry. $z$ is odd under parity, so it connects only states of opposite parity ($\ell$ even ↔ odd), and it does not change $m$ (it commutes with $L_z$). In the $n=2$ space ($2s$; $2p$ with $m=-1,0,1$) the only pair with opposite parity and equal $m$ is $2s\leftrightarrow2p_{m=0}$.

steps.reveal: $\langle200|z|210\rangle=-3a_0$ (radial integral with the given $\Psi_{2,0,0}$, $\Psi_{2,1,0}$).
steps.explain: The angular integral of $\cos\theta$ between the $\ell=0$ and $\ell=1,m=0$ harmonics gives $1/\sqrt3$; the radial integral of $r\cdot R_{20}R_{21}r^2$ gives the rest. Together $-3a_0$: the size of the effect is set by the Bohr radius.

steps.reveal: The $2\times2$ block $\begin{pmatrix}0&3eEa_0\\3eEa_0&0\end{pmatrix}$: $\Delta E=\pm3|e|Ea_0$ for $\frac1{\sqrt2}(|200\rangle\mp|210\rangle)$ (signs depend on the convention for $e$); $|21\pm1\rangle$ unshifted. A linear Stark effect, because of the $\ell$ degeneracy of hydrogen.
steps.explain: Degenerate perturbation theory: inside a degenerate level, diagonalise the perturbation matrix. A $2\times2$ block with zeros on the diagonal has eigenvalues $\pm$(off-diagonal), with eigenvectors $(1,\pm1)/\sqrt2$. The mixed $s$–$p$ states have a permanent dipole moment, hence a shift linear in $E$; this only happens because $2s$ and $2p$ have the same energy in hydrogen.

enc.title: Sheet 14 Q3: Spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman effect

source.where: Exercise sheet XIV, Question 3; official solution: Solutions 14.pdf

enc.goal: $\Delta H=H_{SO}+H_Z=\frac{1}{2m_e^2c^2}\frac1r\frac{dV}{dr}\vec L\cdot\vec S+\frac{\mu_BB_z}{\hbar}(L_z+2S_z)$. (i) Paschen-Back: $H_Z$ dominates; first-order spin-orbit shift; how large must $B_z$ be? (ii) Both as perturbation: diagonalise the $2\times2$ blocks. (iii) For $B_z=0$ recover spin-orbit; to first order in $B_z$ show $\Delta E=g_{\ell j}\mu_BB_zm_j$ with $g_{\ell,\ell\pm1/2}=\frac{2\ell+1\pm1}{2\ell+1}$.

steps.reveal: Basis $|n\ell mm_s\rangle$: $E=\mu_BB_z(m+2m_s)+\xi_{n\ell}\hbar^2mm_s$, with $\xi_{n\ell}=\frac{e^2}{2m_e^2c^2}\langle r^{-3}\rangle$ and $\langle r^{-3}\rangle=\frac{1}{a_0^3n^3\ell(\ell+\frac12)(\ell+1)}$ (only $L_zS_z$ of $\vec L\cdot\vec S$ has diagonal elements). Valid when $\mu_BB\gg$ fine-structure splitting $\sim\alpha^2\mathrm{Ry}/n^3$: of order a tesla or more.
steps.explain: Strong field: the Zeeman term is the big one, and it is diagonal in $|n\ell mm_s\rangle$. Treat spin-orbit as the perturbation: first order needs its diagonal elements. $\vec L\cdot\vec S=L_zS_z+\frac12(L_+S_-+L_-S_+)$ and the $\pm$ terms change $m$ and $m_s$, so only $L_zS_z$ survives on the diagonal: $\hbar^2mm_s$. Valid when the Zeeman splitting exceeds the fine structure.

steps.reveal: $[\vec L^2,\Delta H]=[L_z+S_z,\Delta H]=0$: for fixed $\ell$ and $m_j=m+m_s$ only $|m_j-\frac12,\uparrow\rangle$, $|m_j+\frac12,\downarrow\rangle$ mix; diagonalising each $2\times2$ block gives the Breit-Rabi type formulas interpolating between weak and strong field.
steps.explain: Which states mix: $\Delta H$ commutes with $\vec L^2$ and with $J_z=L_z+S_z$, so it only mixes states with the same $\ell$ and the same $m_j$. For given $m_j$ there are at most two: $|m_j-\frac12,\uparrow\rangle$ and $|m_j+\frac12,\downarrow\rangle$. Diagonalise each $2\times2$ block exactly; this covers all field strengths at once.

steps.reveal: $B=0$: $\vec L\cdot\vec S=\frac{\hbar^2}2[j(j+1)-\ell(\ell+1)-\frac34]$. First order in $B$: $\langle L_z+2S_z\rangle=\hbar m_j\left(1+\frac{\langle\vec S\cdot\vec J\rangle}{\hbar^2j(j+1)}\right)$ (projection theorem), giving $g=\frac{2\ell+2}{2\ell+1}$ for $j=\ell+\frac12$ and $\frac{2\ell}{2\ell+1}$ for $j=\ell-\frac12$.
steps.explain: Weak field: start from spin-orbit eigenstates $|j,m_j\rangle$, where $\vec L\cdot\vec S=\frac12(\vec J^2-\vec L^2-\vec S^2)$ is diagonal. Zeeman at first order needs $\langle L_z+2S_z\rangle=\langle J_z+S_z\rangle$; by the projection theorem $\vec S$ averages to its component along $\vec J$. This gives the Landé factor: each $j$ level splits into $2j+1$ equally spaced lines.
